docs.title: Data Streams and Transmission Modes
docs.text:
Unit 1Notes2 min read

This page covers syllabus item 1.3, data stream characteristics for traditional and continuous media.

docs.title: Serial transmission
docs.text: Multimedia communication is generally transmitted serially: one bit at a time. The three modes below differ in how the receiver stays in step with the sender.

docs.title: Asynchronous transmission
docs.text:
• Synchronization at the byte level.
  • There may be gaps between bytes, which makes it good for random communication.
  • Examples: WWW, e-mail, keyboard.

Extra

Because there is no shared clock, each byte is wrapped with a start bit and a stop bit so the receiver knows where it begins and ends. That is why the textbook notes that synchronous transmission has no start and stop bits.

docs.title: Synchronous transmission
docs.text:
• No start and stop bits.
  • Sender and receiver must be synchronized, using clocks.

docs.title: Isochronous transmission
docs.text:
• Data is transferred at a fixed rate.
  • It delivers data at a steady rate.
  • It is best for multimedia communication.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Asynchronous Synchronous Isochronous Timing unit Byte level Clock shared by sender and receiver Fixed, steady rate Gaps allowed? Yes, between bytes Clock-driven Data arrives at a steady rate Start/stop bits Used (implied) None Not specified Best for Random, bursty traffic Clock-aligned transfer Multimedia Examples WWW, e-mail, keyboard – Audio and video streams

docs.title: Why multimedia needs a steady rate
docs.text:
Continuous media only make sense if they arrive on time and in order: a late audio sample is a click, a late video frame is a stutter. That is why it is called isochronous transfer "best for multimedia", and why the challenges of latency, delay and synchronization keep returning (see The Multimedia System).

Do not confuse these

Synchronization (the cross-domain layer that coordinates media in time) is not the same as synchronous transmission (a transmission mode where sender and receiver share a clock). Name each one clearly in your answers.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
Which transmission mode is best for multimedia, and why?

Isochronous, because it transfers data at a fixed, steady rate, which is what continuous media such as audio and video need.

Give two differences between asynchronous and synchronous transmission.

Asynchronous synchronizes at the byte level and allows gaps between bytes (e.g. keyboard, e-mail, WWW). Synchronous uses no start and stop bits and needs sender and receiver to be synchronized with clocks.

Is the synchronization layer in the global structure the same as synchronous transmission?

No. The synchronization layer coordinates different media in time across all domains (for example audio with video). Synchronous transmission is a mode of sending data in which sender and receiver share a clock.

docs.title: Global Structure of Multimedia
docs.text:
Unit 1Notes4 min read

Exam tip

This is the one diagram you are most likely to be asked to draw and explain. Practise redrawing it from memory until you can place every box.

docs.title: The big picture
docs.text:
The global structure of multimedia is a framework that covers the devices, systems, applications and interactions needed to capture, process, store, transmit and present media in a cohesive and interactive way.

It has three domains and one cross-domain layer:

  1. Application domain (top)
  2. System domain (middle)
  3. Device domain (bottom)
  4. Synchronization, a vertical layer that runs through all three
flowchart TB
    subgraph A["Application Domain"]
        direction LR
        A0["Tools and Applications"]
        A1["Documents"]
        A2["User Interface"]
        A3["Programming Abstractions"]
    end
    subgraph S["System Domain"]
        direction LR
        S1["Database Systems"]
        S2["Operating Systems"]
        S3["Communication Systems"]
        S4["Computer Technology"]
    end
    subgraph D["Device Domain"]
        direction LR
        D1["Storage"]
        D2["Compression"]
        D3["Network"]
        D4["Sound"]
        D5["Image / Graphics"]
        D6["Video / Animation"]
    end
    A --> S --> D
    Y["Synchronization (cross domain)"] -.-> A
    Y -.-> S
    Y -.-> D

In the usual diagram the three domains are stacked as boxes, with a tall vertical bar labelled Synchronization along the left side that spans all three.

Layer Boxes in the diagram Application domain Tools and Applications (full-width bar); below it Documents, User Interface, Programming Abstractions System domain Database Systems, Operating Systems, Communication Systems; below them a full-width bar, Computer Technology Device domain Storage, Compression and Network; under Compression: Sound, Image/Graphics, Video/Animation

docs.title: Application domain
docs.text:
Provides the functions the user needs to develop and present multimedia projects. It includes software tools and a project-development methodology. The services of the system domain are offered to it through programming abstractions.

End-user software: media players, video editors, animation tools, presentation software.

  • Documents. Multimedia-enhanced documents that combine text, images, audio and video: e-learning materials, interactive PDFs, web pages. Document handling means generating the different media and recording them at presentation time.
  • User interface. Lets people interact with the system: buttons, menus, touch interfaces. It must be intuitive, responsive and multimedia-friendly.
  • Programming abstractions. APIs, libraries and frameworks (media APIs, graphics libraries, game engines) that spare developers low-level complexity.

docs.title: System domain
docs.text:
Includes all the support for using the functions of the device domain: operating systems, communication systems (networking) and database systems. Computer technology is the layer that connects the device domain to the system domain.

  • Database systems. Store and manage multimedia objects (audio, video, images) with support for searching, indexing and retrieval. Example: multimedia databases for video libraries and digital archives. They also allow structured access to large databases.
  • Operating systems. Manage the resources multimedia needs: CPU, memory, disk and I/O devices. They provide real-time scheduling and device drivers (sound card, graphics card). Examples: Windows, Linux, macOS.
  • Communication systems. Handle data exchange between systems with protocols and data synchronization. Examples: TCP/IP and RTP (for real-time media). They are responsible for data transmission.

docs.title: Device domain
docs.text:
Covers the basic concepts and skills for processing the media elements and handling physical devices: cameras, microphones, speakers and other input/output hardware. It includes the processing of digital signals, image, graphics, animation, audio and video.

  • Compression. Raw multimedia data is very large. Compression reduces its size for faster transmission and efficient storage. Examples: MP3, AAC (audio), JPEG, PNG (image), MPEG, H.264 (video). It is essential for streaming, video conferencing and multimedia applications.
  • Network. Carries multimedia data between systems for streaming, online video calls and distributed applications. It requires high bandwidth and low latency.
  • Storage. Holds content permanently or temporarily: hard disks, SSDs, cloud storage. It must support large data volumes and fast read/write.

docs.title: The synchronization layer (cross domain)
docs.text:
A vertical layer that affects all levels of the system. Synchronization is the coordination of multiple media types in time.

  • Audio must match video during playback.
  • Subtitles must appear at the correct moments.
  • It is critical for video conferencing, movies and e-learning.
  • Poor synchronization causes audio-video mismatch and a poor user experience.

Some sources call this layer the cross domain: it handles the temporal relationships among media across all domains. Unit 10 is devoted to it.

docs.title: Where students go wrong
docs.text:
Network appears twice

Network (the physical carrier, needing bandwidth and low latency) is in the device domain. Communication systems (protocols such as TCP/IP and RTP) are in the system domain. Do not put compression, storage or network in the system domain.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
Name the three domains from top to bottom and one component of each.

Application (e.g. user interface), System (e.g. operating systems), Device (e.g. compression). The vertical synchronization layer runs across all of them.

Why does synchronization sit across all domains rather than in one?

Because timing between media must be preserved at every level: when devices capture and play, when the OS schedules, when the network delivers and when the application presents. A mismatch at any level breaks the experience (for example, lips out of sync with audio).

In which domain does the operating system belong, and what two services does it give multimedia?

The system domain. It provides real-time scheduling and device drivers (for example for the sound or graphics card), while managing CPU, memory, disk and I/O.

docs.title: Classification of Media
docs.text:
Unit 1Notes3 min read

Exam tip

This is the most examinable block of the unit. Expect a direct question such as "Classify media" or "Explain the types of media with examples".

A medium is the means for distribution and presentation of information. Media can be classified by different criteria. These notes use six categories, each defined by a central question.

Remember it by asking the question

If you cannot decide which category something belongs to, ask each central question in turn. The one that fits is the answer.

docs.title: The six categories at a glance
docs.text: Medium Central question Examples Perception How do humans perceive information in a computer environment? Seeing: text, image, video. Hearing: music, noise, speech. Representation How is the information coded in the computer? ASCII, JPEG, PCM, PAL/NTSC/SECAM, MPEG Presentation Through which devices is information delivered to and introduced into the computer? Output: paper, screen, speaker. Input: keyboard, mouse, camera, microphone. Storage How will information be stored? Hard disk, CD-ROM, SSD, floppy disk, microfilm Transmission Over what will information be transmitted? Coaxial cable, fibre optics, free air space (wireless) Information exchange Which carrier is used to exchange information between places? Storage plus transmission combined, e.g. e-mail

docs.title: Perception medium
docs.text:
Perception media help humans sense their environment. The answer to the central question is: through seeing and hearing.

  • Seeing: text, image and video.
  • Hearing: music, noise and speech.

docs.title: Representation medium
docs.text:
Defined by the internal computer representation of information: the formats used to code each kind of media.

  • Text is coded in ASCII .
  • Graphics are coded according to the CEPT or CAPTAIN videotext standards.
  • Images can be stored in JPEG format.
  • Audio streams are coded with PCM .
  • Audio-video sequences can be coded in different TV standards (PAL, NTSC, SECAM) and stored in the computer in MPEG format.

docs.title: Presentation medium
docs.text:
The tools and devices for the input and output of information.

  • Output media: paper, screen, speaker.
  • Input media: keyboard, mouse, camera, microphone.

docs.title: Storage medium
docs.text: The data carrier that enables storage of information: hard disk, CD-ROM and similar. Microfilm, floppy disk and SSD also count.

docs.title: Transmission medium
docs.text: The different information carriers that enable continuous data transmission: coaxial cable, fibre optics, and free air space, which is used for wireless traffic.

docs.title: Information exchange medium
docs.text:
Includes all information carriers for transmission: that is, all storage and transmission media. Information can be exchanged by transporting a storage medium to the destination, or through computer networks such as an electronic mailing system.

Watch out

Some summaries list the information exchange medium as "VR, Cloud, Internet". The full definition is storage plus transmission media, for example e-mail. Use the full definition in the exam.

docs.title: Common confusions
docs.text: Mistake Correct reading "A monitor is a perception medium." A monitor is a presentation medium. Perception is the human sense (eyes, ears). "E-mail is a transmission medium." E-mail is an information exchange medium: it combines storage and transmission. "JPEG is a storage medium." JPEG is a representation format. The disk that holds the file is the storage medium. "A cable stores data." A cable is a transmission medium; it only carries data.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
A speaker is used to play a song. Which medium class is the speaker, and which is the song as heard?

The speaker is a presentation (output) medium. The song as heard by the ear is a perception medium (hearing).

Which medium answers 'How is the information coded in the computer?' and give two examples.

The representation medium: for example ASCII for text and JPEG for images (also PCM for audio, PAL/NTSC/SECAM and MPEG for video).

Explain the information exchange medium with an example.

It covers all storage and transmission media: information can travel by moving a storage medium to the destination, or over a network. An electronic mailing system is the course example.

docs.title: Media Concepts and Properties
docs.text:
Unit 1Notes3 min read

This page covers the part of syllabus item 1.2 that deals with properties and notation. The syllabus never uses the word notation; the closest material is Media Concepts, the three things every medium defines.

docs.title: Media concepts
docs.text:
Each medium defines:

  1. Representation space
  2. Representation values
  3. Representation dimensions

docs.title: Representation space
docs.text:
The surrounding where the media are presented.

  • Visual representation space: paper, screen.
  • Acoustic representation space: mono, stereo.

docs.title: Representation values
docs.text:
Determine how the information is represented.

  • Continuous values: for example electromagnetic waves.
  • Discrete values: for example text characters in digital form.

docs.title: Representation dimensions
docs.text:
A representation space has a spatial dimension and a temporal dimension.

  • Spatial dimension: two-dimensional (a monitor) or three-dimensional (holography).
  • Temporal dimension:
    • Time-independent media are discrete media. The information is a sequence of individual elements with no time component. Example: a document.
    • Time-dependent media are continuous media. Information is expressed not only by its individual values but also by its time of occurrence. Example: a movie.
Discrete media Continuous media Time component None (time-independent) Essential (time-dependent) Information is A sequence of individual elements Values and the time at which they occur Examples Text, still images, a document Audio, video, a movie

Same words, two meanings

These notes use "continuous" and "discrete" for representation values (a continuous wave versus a digital character) and again for media types by time dependence. In an exam, say which one you mean. The "text plus pictures is not multimedia" argument below uses the time-dependence meaning.

docs.title: Properties of a multimedia system
docs.text: "Multimedia" is not any arbitrary combination of media. A multimedia system has three main properties.

docs.title: 1. Combination of media
docs.text: A simple text-processing program that incorporates images is often called a multimedia application, because two media are handled by one program. But one should speak of multimedia only when both continuous and discrete media are utilised. So a text processor with pictures is not a multimedia application.

docs.title: 2. Independence
docs.text:
An important aspect of different media is their level of independence from each other. In general independence of different media is requested, but multimedia may require several levels of independence.

  • Tightly coupled: a computer-controlled video recorder stores audio and video together. There is an inherent, tight connection between the two media, coupled through a common storage medium.
  • Independent: for presentation, the combination of DAT (digital audio tape recorder) signals and computer-available text satisfies the request for media independence.

docs.title: 3. Computer-supported integration
docs.text: The computer is an ideal tool for media combination. The system should be capable of computer-controlled media processing, and should be programmable by a system programmer or even by the user.

docs.title: Properties versus characteristics
docs.text:
Do not mix this page up with The Multimedia System.

Three properties (this page) Four characteristics Names Combination of media, independence, computer-supported integration Computer controlled, integrated, digitally represented, interactive Focus What makes a combination of media a multimedia system What a multimedia system is like in operation

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
Is a word processor with embedded photographs a multimedia application? Why or why not?

No. Text and photographs are both discrete (time-independent) media. Multimedia needs both discrete and continuous media, so adding an audio clip or video would make it a multimedia application.

Explain discrete versus continuous media with one example each.

Discrete media have no time component and are a sequence of individual elements (a text document). Continuous media are time-dependent: information is expressed by its values and by when they occur (a movie).

What does 'independence' mean for media in a multimedia system?

The degree to which media can be handled separately from one another. A video recorder stores audio and video tightly coupled on a common storage medium, whereas DAT audio signals combined with computer text for presentation are independent.

docs.title: The Multimedia System
docs.text: Unit 1Notes3 min read

docs.title: What is a multimedia system?
docs.text:
Two common wordings:

  • A multimedia system is a system capable of processing multimedia data and applications. It is characterised by the processing, storage, generation and manipulation of multimedia information.
  • A system that involves generation, representation, storage, transmission, search and retrieval of multimedia information. It also involves processing and analysis, including compression, and includes multimedia hardware, software and network.

docs.title: The four basic characteristics
docs.text:
Exam tip

This is one of the most repeated topics: the four characteristics are always asked. Learn the four names and one supporting detail for each.

# Characteristic What it means 1 Computer controlled A computer controls every stage: producing content with image, sound and video editors; storing large shared information; transmitting it over a network; and presenting it through display, speakers or projector. 2 Integrated All components (text, audio, video, pictures, graphics, animation) are integrated. Devices such as the camera and microphone are connected to, and controlled by, a single computer. Digital storage is used for all media types, and the information is shown on the computer screen. 3 Digitally represented Analog signals must be converted to digital signals. Digital signals can be processed very effectively. 4 Interactive The final presentation is usually interactive: the user can select the time, order and speed of the presentation and can modify the content.

docs.title: Challenges of multimedia computing
docs.text:
• Synchronization: maintaining the temporal relationship between different media types.
  • Sequencing: playing frames in the correct order and within the correct time frame.
  • Distributed networks: latency and delay over a network.
  • Storage and bandwidth: continuous media such as video need a lot of space to store and very high bandwidth to transmit.
  • Complex algorithms and hardware: multimedia spans many research areas and needs more complex and more efficient algorithms and hardware platforms.
  • Automatic analysis and indexing: analysing and indexing audio, image and video is much harder than for text.

docs.title: Desirable features of a multimedia system
docs.text: Area Feature Processing Very high processing power for large data and real-time delivery Software A multimedia file system for audio and video streaming; software tools to handle and deliver media Hardware Special hardware such as RAID; high, efficient I/O for real-time recording and playback Compression Compression and decompression in real time Capacity Storage in the order of terabytes, memory in the order of gigabytes, large caches and high-speed buses Network Network support for client-server and distributed systems

docs.title: Components of a multimedia system
docs.text:
Component Examples Capture devices Video camera, video recorder, microphone, keyboards and mice, graphics tablets, 3D input devices, tactile sensors, VR devices, digitising hardware Storage devices Hard disks, SSD, CD-ROM, DVD, Blu-ray Communication networks Local networks, intranets, internet, Gigabit Ethernet, special high-speed networks Computer system Multimedia desktop machines and workstations, processor, RAM, sound card, display card, MPEG/video/DSP hardware Display devices High-resolution monitors, speakers, projector, HDTV, SVGA, colour printers

Capture, storage, communication, computing and display form a chain: media are captured, stored, sent, processed and shown.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
List the four basic characteristics of a multimedia system.

Computer controlled, integrated, digitally represented, interactive (the final presentation is usually interactive).

Why is digital representation so important?

Analog signals must be converted to digital so one computer can store, process, transmit and combine all media. Digital signals can also be processed very effectively.

Why are continuous media such as video a challenge?

They need large storage and very high bandwidth, and their parts must stay in the correct order and time relationship (synchronization and sequencing), even across a network with latency and delay.

docs.title: Unit 1: Practice Questions
docs.text:
Unit 1Practice6 min read

Write your own answer on paper first, then click to reveal the model answer. Marks are a guide to how much detail the question deserves.

docs.title: Short answer
docs.text:
1. Define multimedia and medium. (3 marks)

A medium is the means for distribution and presentation of information (text, graphics, speech, music, video).

Multimedia is the computer-controlled integration of text, graphics, drawings, still and moving images, animation, audio and any other media, where every type of information can be represented, stored, transmitted and processed digitally, and is usually delivered interactively.

2. List the five building blocks of multimedia and describe any two. (4 marks)

Text, audio, graphics, video, animation.

Example descriptions: Audio is produced by vibration and perceived by hearing; in multimedia it takes the form of speech, effects and music. Animation is the rapid display of a sequence of images of 2D artwork or model positions to create an illusion of movement, due to persistence of vision.

3. State the four basic characteristics of a multimedia system. (4 marks)
  1. Computer controlled: the computer controls production, storage, transmission and presentation.
  2. Integrated: all media and devices are integrated and controlled by one computer; digital storage is used for all media types.
  3. Digitally represented: analog signals are converted to digital, which can be processed effectively.
  4. Interactive: the user can choose the time, order and speed of presentation and can modify content.
4. Why is a text processor with embedded images not a multimedia application? (3 marks)

Text and still images are both discrete (time-independent) media. Multimedia requires the use of both discrete and continuous (time-dependent, such as audio and video) media. Adding an audio or video clip would make it multimedia.

5. Differentiate asynchronous, synchronous and isochronous transmission. (5 marks)
  • Asynchronous: synchronization at the byte level; gaps between bytes are possible; good for random communication (WWW, e-mail, keyboard).
  • Synchronous: no start and stop bits; sender and receiver must be synchronized with clocks.
  • Isochronous: data is transferred at a fixed, steady rate; best for multimedia communication.
6. What is the role of the synchronization layer in the global structure? (3 marks)

It is a vertical, cross-domain layer that coordinates multiple media types in time: audio must match video, subtitles must appear at the right moment. It is critical for video conferencing, movies and e-learning. Poor synchronization causes audio-video mismatch and a poor user experience.

docs.title: Long answer
docs.text:
7. Draw and explain the global structure of multimedia. (8 marks)

Draw three stacked domains with a tall vertical Synchronization bar spanning them.

  • Application domain: tools and applications, documents, user interface, programming abstractions. It lets users develop and present multimedia projects; system services reach it through programming abstractions.
  • System domain: operating systems (CPU, memory, disk and I/O management, real-time scheduling, device drivers), database systems (store, search, index, retrieve multimedia objects), communication systems (protocols such as TCP/IP and RTP), on top of computer technology.
  • Device domain: storage, compression, network, and the media hardware for sound, image/graphics and video/animation.
  • Synchronization (cross domain): temporal coordination of media across all domains.
8. Explain the classification of media with examples. (8 marks)

Six categories, each with a central question:

Medium Central question Examples Perception How do humans perceive information? Seeing (text, image, video); hearing (music, noise, speech) Representation How is information coded in the computer? ASCII, JPEG, PCM, PAL/NTSC/SECAM, MPEG Presentation Through which devices is information delivered and introduced? Output: paper, screen, speaker. Input: keyboard, mouse, camera, microphone Storage How is information stored? Hard disk, CD-ROM, SSD Transmission Over what is information transmitted? Coaxial cable, fibre optics, free air space Information exchange Which carrier moves information between places? Storage plus transmission, e.g. e-mail 9. Explain the challenges of multimedia computing and the desirable features of a multimedia system. (6 marks)

Challenges: synchronization; sequencing; latency and delay on distributed networks; large storage and very high bandwidth for continuous media; complex algorithms and hardware; automatic analysis and indexing of audio, image and video is harder than for text.

Desirable features: very high processing power and real-time delivery; a multimedia file system; special hardware such as RAID; real-time compression and decompression; efficient I/O; terabytes of storage and gigabytes of memory with large caches and fast buses; network support for client-server and distributed use; software tools to handle and deliver media.

docs.title: Multiple choice
docs.text:
10. Which pairing is correct?
  • A. Perception medium: how information is coded in the computer
  • B. Presentation medium: the devices through which information is delivered to and introduced into the computer
  • C. Storage medium: what information is transmitted over
  • D. Information exchange medium: how humans sense information

Answer: B. A describes the representation medium, C the transmission medium, and D the perception medium.

11. A monitor is best classified as a
  • A. Perception medium
  • B. Representation medium
  • C. Presentation medium
  • D. Transmission medium

Answer: C. A screen is an output (presentation) device. Perception is the human sense that receives the image.

12. Which of these is a continuous (time-dependent) medium?
  • A. A text document
  • B. A still photograph
  • C. A movie
  • D. A page of ASCII characters

Answer: C. A movie's information depends on its time of occurrence. The others have no time component.

13. Which transmission mode is best for multimedia?
  • A. Asynchronous
  • B. Synchronous
  • C. Isochronous
  • D. Parallel

Answer: C. Isochronous transfer is at a fixed, steady rate. Asynchronous allows gaps between bytes; synchronous removes start and stop bits and relies on shared clocks; parallel is not one of the three modes, and multimedia communication is generally serial.

14. In the global structure, compression, storage and network belong to the
  • A. Application domain
  • B. System domain
  • C. Device domain
  • D. Synchronization layer

Answer: C. The system domain holds operating, database and communication systems; the application domain holds tools, documents, user interface and programming abstractions.

15. Which is NOT one of the four basic characteristics of a multimedia system?
  • A. Computer controlled
  • B. Integrated
  • C. Analog representation
  • D. Interactive

Answer: C. Multimedia information must be represented digitally.

16. Which of these correctly describes asynchronous transmission?
  • A. No start and stop bits, clock-synchronized
  • B. Synchronization at the byte level, with possible gaps between bytes
  • C. Fixed-rate delivery
  • D. Parallel bit transfer

Answer: B. A describes synchronous, C isochronous. D is not a transmission mode.

17. Which statement about 'combination of media' is correct?
  • A. Any two media make a multimedia application
  • B. Multimedia requires both continuous and discrete media
  • C. Multimedia requires at least three discrete media
  • D. Multimedia requires only continuous media

Answer: B. That is why a text processor with pictures (both discrete) is not multimedia.

docs.title: What Is Multimedia?
docs.text: Unit 1Notes5 min read

docs.title: Medium and multimedia
docs.text:
The word is built from multi (many, much, multiple) and medium.

A medium is the means for distribution and presentation of information. Text, graphics, speech, music and video are all media. Media can be classified by different criteria; the classification by perception (what the human senses: text, audio, video) is the one that suits the definition of multimedia. The full six-way classification is in Classification of Media.

docs.title: Three definitions to know
docs.text:
Version Definition Short A combination of text, graphics, sound, animation and video delivered interactively to the user by electronic or digitally manipulated means. Field-based The field concerned with the computer-controlled integration of text, graphics, drawings, still and moving images (video), animation, audio and any other media, where every type of information can be represented, stored, transmitted and processed digitally. Digital-information Digital information represented through audio, video and animation, in addition to traditional media such as text, graphics and images; an integration of these media, stored, transmitted and processed digitally.

All three agree on the same core ideas: integration of several media, digital representation, and (in the first definition) interactive delivery.

Exam tip

A full-mark definition names all three ideas: integration of media, digital representation/processing, and interactivity. Writing only "many media together" earns partial marks.

docs.title: The building blocks
docs.text: Every multimedia application is assembled from five elements.

docs.title: Text
docs.text: Text and symbols are essential for communication. With the growth of the Internet and the WWW, text matters more than ever. The Web began as HTML, originally designed to display simple text documents on screens.

docs.title: Audio
docs.text: Audio is produced by vibration and perceived by the sense of hearing. In multimedia it appears as speech, sound effects and music.

docs.title: Graphics
docs.text: A graphic is a two-dimensional figure or illustration. It may be produced manually (drawing, painting, carving) or by computer graphics technology. In multimedia, graphics show more clearly what the information is about: diagrams and pictures.

docs.title: Video
docs.text: Video is the technology of capturing, recording, processing, transmitting and reconstructing moving pictures. It consumes a lot of storage, so plan its use carefully.

docs.title: Animation
docs.text:
Animation is the rapid display of a sequence of images of 2D artwork or model positions to create an illusion of movement. It is an optical illusion caused by persistence of vision.

Extra

Persistence of vision means the eye keeps an image for a short moment after it disappears, so frames shown quickly one after another blend into smooth motion.

Element What it is Key idea to remember Text Symbols and characters HTML began as simple text display Audio Vibration heard by the ear Speech, effects, music Graphics 2D figures and illustrations Drawn by hand or by computer Video Moving pictures captured and reconstructed Needs large storage Animation Rapid sequence of images Persistence of vision

docs.title: History
docs.text: Period Milestones Early beginning Artist Bob Goldstein coined the term "multimedia" for his 1966 show Lightworks at L'Oursin. 1970s–1980s 1972: Atari's Pong, one of the earliest examples combining graphics and sound. 1976: Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak founded Apple. 1977: the Apple II, which used colour graphics. 1981: IBM PC. 1984: Apple Macintosh with a graphical user interface (GUI) and mouse. 1990s "Multimedia" was probably one of the most overused terms of the decade. The field sat at the crossroads of computing, telecommunications, publishing, consumer audio-video electronics, and television/movie/broadcasting. 2000s–present The Internet and streaming services made multimedia more accessible and interactive. Virtual reality, augmented reality and interactive media give more immersive experiences.

docs.title: Aspects of multimedia
docs.text: Aspect Meaning Interactivity Interaction between users and content: clicking, dragging, entering text. Integration Different media types combined into one cohesive application. Hyperlinking Pieces of content connected by links, as on websites. User control The user controls pace and flow: pause, play, skip. Multisensory experience Engages several senses: sight, hearing, touch.

docs.title: Linear and non-linear multimedia
docs.text:
• Linear content runs in a fixed order that the user cannot change, such as a book read page by page or a film.
  • Non-linear multimedia is interactive: the user has control over the content. Examples are games and interactive video.

Hypertext is text meant to be read non-linearly by following links. Hypermedia extends the links beyond text to graphics, images, sound and video. The World Wide Web is the best example.

A common diagram contrasts an open book labelled linear with a stack of pages joined by curved arrows through red "hot spots" labelled hypertext, non-linear.

Extra

Hypertext, hypermedia and the standards behind them return in Unit 9.

docs.title: Multimedia applications
docs.text:
• One common list: WWW, education, medicine, communication, broadcasting, entertainment and games, industry, commercial.
  • Another list: digital video editing, electronic newspaper, WWW, games, encyclopedia, home shopping, interactive TV, video conferencing, video on demand.

Two typical illustrations: a desktop video-conference set-up, and an MPEG-4 delivery diagram in which a live camera and encoder feed an IP network that reaches wired PCs, GPRS/EDGE/3G phones and a home RF network, with servers and embedded players at the edges.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
Why is 'a combination of many media' not a complete definition of multimedia?

Because the textbook's definitions also require that the media be integrated under computer control, represented digitally, and (usually) delivered interactively. A slideshow of printed photos beside a radio is many media, but not multimedia.

Which element depends on persistence of vision?

Animation: a rapid sequence of still images that the eye blends into apparent motion.

Give one example each of linear and non-linear presentation.

Linear: a film or a printed book. Non-linear: a video game or an interactive video, where the user's choices change what happens next.

docs.title: Unit 2: Sound and Audio
docs.text:
4 hours · weeks 2–3 · syllabus items 2.1 (sound and music) and 2.2 (speech)

Unit 1 told you what multimedia is. This unit starts the tour of the individual media with the one you can hear: sound. You will learn what sound physically is, how a computer turns it into numbers, how music is described as instructions (MIDI) instead of samples, and how computers generate, analyse and transmit human speech.

Open the class slides

docs.title: What you must master
docs.text:
1. Define sound, waveform, period, frequency and amplitude, and give the frequency ranges.
  2. Distinguish sound from audio.
  3. Explain how an analog sound wave becomes digital: sampling, the Nyquist theorem and quantization, and calculate file size with the formula.
  4. Describe MIDI: the two parts of the interface, messages, devices, channels, and the MIDI versus SMPTE timing difference.
  5. Explain speech generation (time-dependent and frequency-dependent concatenation, formants) and the two steps of speech synthesis.
  6. Explain speech analysis (who, what, how) and speech recognition.
  7. Explain speech transmission (PCM, source encoding, recognition/synthesis) and compare the common audio file formats.

These weights are estimates based on how much space each topic usually gets. They are not from a past paper.

Most likely questions

  • Sampling, Nyquist theorem, quantization and the file-size calculation.
  • MIDI: what it is, its two components, messages, devices and channels; and MIDI versus SMPTE (it was set as an assignment).
  • Speech generation: time-dependent versus frequency-dependent concatenation, and the two steps of speech synthesis.

docs.title: Digital Audio and File Formats
docs.text: Unit 2Notes4 min read

docs.title: Computer representation of sound
docs.text:
The smooth, continuous curve of a sound wave cannot be stored directly in a computer. Instead:

  1. The computer measures the amplitude of the waveform at regular time intervals.
  2. This produces a series of numbers called samples.
  3. The conversion is done by an Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC).
  4. The reverse is done by a Digital-to-Analog Converter (DAC).

An example of an ADC is the AM79C30A digital subscriber controller chip. A typical diagram shows the smooth pressure wave on the left and, on the right, the same wave as a row of vertical bars (the samples) whose heights follow the wave.

flowchart LR
    A["Sound wave (analog)"] --> B["Microphone / transducer"]
    B --> C["ADC: sample and quantize"]
    C --> D["Digital samples (numbers)"]
    D --> E["DAC"]
    E --> F["Speaker: sound wave"]

docs.title: Sampling rate
docs.text:
The rate at which a continuous waveform is sampled is the sampling rate, measured in hertz.

Nyquist sampling theorem

For lossless digitization, the sampling rate should be at least twice the maximum frequency response.

Example. The CD standard sampling rate is 44,100 Hz: the waveform is sampled 44,100 times per second. A rate of 44,100 Hz can only represent frequencies up to 22,050 Hz, which is why it covers the audible range up to 20 kHz.

\[f_s \ge 2 f_{max} \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f_{max} \le \frac{f_s}{2}\]

docs.title: Quantization
docs.text:
The value of each sample must be stored as a discrete number. The resolution (quantization) of a sample depends on the number of bits used to measure the height of the waveform.

Bits per sample Number of levels Example 3-bit 2³ = 8 An illustration of coarse quantization 8-bit 2⁸ = 256 Lower quality 16-bit 2¹⁶ = 65,536 CD quality

The lower the quantization, the lower the quality of the sound.

Controls More means Sampling rate How often the wave is measured (time axis) Higher frequencies captured Quantization (bits) How precisely each measurement is stored (amplitude axis) Finer loudness detail

docs.title: Quality versus file size
docs.text:
The size of a digital recording depends on the sampling rate, the resolution and the number of channels. Higher sampling rate and higher resolution give higher quality but a bigger file.

\[S = R \times \frac{b}{8} \times C \times D\] Symbol Meaning Unit S File size bytes R Sampling rate samples per second b Resolution bits C Channels 1 = mono, 2 = stereo D Recording duration seconds

Note: 1 KB = 1024 bytes and 1 MB = 1024 KB.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
Record 10 seconds of stereo music at 44.1 kHz, 16 bits.

\[S = 44100 \times \frac{16}{8} \times 2 \times 10 = 1{,}764{,}000\ \text{bytes} = 1722.7\ \text{KB} \approx 1.68\ \text{MB}\]

High-quality sound files are very big, but the size can be reduced by compression.

Extra: two extra practice calculations

  • Mono, 8 kHz, 8-bit, 1 minute: S = 8000 × (8/8) × 1 × 60 = 480,000 bytes ≈ 468.75 KB.
  • Stereo, 44.1 kHz, 16-bit, 3 minutes (180 s): S = 44100 × (16/8) × 2 × 180 = 31,752,000 bytes ≈ 30.3 MB.

Exam tip

Always show the formula, substitute each value with its unit, and convert at the end (÷1024 for KB, ÷1024 again for MB). Forgetting b/8 (bits to bytes) or the channels is the most common loss of marks.

docs.title: Audio file formats
docs.text: Format Full name / origin Key points WAV Waveform; developed by Microsoft; subset of RIFF Most commonly used on Windows. Offers several encoding methods (including Wave or PCM), so check the player supports the one you use for Internet sound. AU Sun Audio; Sun Microsystems For UNIX, NeXT and Sun SPARC workstations. A 16-bit compressed format, fairly common on the Web because it plays on the widest number of platforms. RA Progressive Networks RealAudio Very popular for streaming on the Internet, with good compression up to a factor of 18. Streaming lets a file start playing before the whole file has downloaded. AIFF Apple's Audio Interchange File Format The Macintosh waveform format; also supported on IBM compatibles and Silicon Graphics. Supports many sampling rates, up to 32 bits. MPEG / MPEG-2 Motion Picture Experts Group Compressed audio and video format, with compression of at least 14:1.

docs.title: Lossy and lossless formats
docs.text: Lossy (smaller size, some quality loss) Lossless (no quality loss, reduced size) Formats MP3 (.mp3, most popular), AAC (.aac, better than MP3 at the same bitrate), OGG Vorbis (.ogg, open-source alternative to MP3), WMA (.wma, Microsoft) FLAC (.flac, popular open source), ALAC (.m4a, Apple Lossless Audio Codec), APE (.ape, Monkey's Audio) Typical use Music streaming, portable devices Archiving, high-quality playback

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
State the Nyquist theorem and use it for a 44,100 Hz sampling rate.

For lossless digitization, the sampling rate must be at least twice the maximum frequency. At 44,100 Hz the highest frequency that can be represented is 22,050 Hz.

Calculate the size of 10 seconds of stereo audio at 44.1 kHz and 16 bits.

S = 44100 × (16/8) × 2 × 10 = 1,764,000 bytes, which is about 1722.7 KB or 1.68 MB.

Why are lossless formats used for archiving but lossy formats for streaming?

Lossless formats (FLAC, ALAC, APE) keep all the original quality while reducing size, so they suit archives. Lossy formats (MP3, AAC, OGG, WMA) give much smaller files with some quality loss, which suits streaming and portable devices.

docs.title: MIDI
docs.text: Unit 2Notes4 min read

docs.title: Why MIDI exists
docs.text:
A sound signal can be stored as a digitised sequence of samples. But music can also be described in a symbolic way, the way a printed score lists notes. Computers and electronic musical instruments use a similar technique, and most of them use MIDI (Musical Instrument Digital Interface), a standard developed in the early 1980s.

  • The MIDI standard defines how to code all the elements of a musical score: sequences of notes, timing conditions, and the instrument that plays each note.
  • It is a set of specifications for instrument development, so instruments from different manufacturers can easily exchange musical information.
  • Each word describing an action in a musical performance is assigned a specific binary code.

Samples versus instructions

Digitised audio stores what the sound looked like (thousands of sample values per second). MIDI stores what to play (which note, how loud, on which instrument). That is why a MIDI file is tiny and why it contains no individual sample values.

docs.title: The two components of a MIDI interface
docs.text:
Component What it does Hardware Connects the equipment. It adds a MIDI port to an instrument, specifies a MIDI cable, and processes the electrical signals over the cable. Data format Encodes the information the hardware processes. It does not encode individual sampling values; instead it uses a specific data format for each instrument, covering the start and end of a score, the basic frequency, the loudness and the instrument itself.

A typical diagram shows a laptop (the digital audio workstation) connected to a synthesizer, a MIDI keyboard and an audio interface with USB, audio and MIDI cables.

docs.title: MIDI messages
docs.text: The MIDI data format is digital, and data are grouped into MIDI messages. When a musician plays a key, the MIDI interface generates a message that defines the start of each note and its intensity. The message is transmitted to the machines connected to the system.

docs.title: MIDI devices, channels and instruments
docs.text:
• An instrument that complies with both components of the MIDI interface (hardware and data format) is a MIDI device. Example: a synthesizer.
  • The MIDI standard specifies 16 channels. A MIDI device is mapped onto a channel.
  • The standard identifies 128 instruments by number, including noise effects such as a phone ringing or an airplane taking off.
Number Instrument 0 Piano 12 Marimba 40 Violin 73 Flute

docs.title: MIDI clock
docs.text:
• Used to synchronise timing between MIDI devices.
  • It keeps all connected devices playing in time with each other, which is crucial for rhythm and tempo in live performances and recordings.
  • As an alternative, the SMPTE clock allows receiver-sender synchronisation.

A number that does not match the MIDI standard

Some sources say the MIDI clock sends 2 timing ticks per quarter note. The MIDI specification itself defines 24 timing clocks per quarter note. Always quote the standard figure of 24 in exams.

docs.title: SMPTE timing code
docs.text:
• Developed by the Society of Motion Picture and Television Engineers.
  • Uses the format hours:minutes:seconds:frames.
  • Typically used in film and television to precisely synchronise audio and video.
  • Requires more bandwidth than a MIDI connection can support, because it carries detailed timing information for each frame.

Format: HH:MM:SS:FF, where HH = hours, MM = minutes, SS = seconds, FF = frames.

Frame rate Used for 24 fps Film 25 fps PAL (Europe, Asia): Phase Alternating Line 29.97 fps NTSC (TV): National Television System Committee 30 fps Video production

docs.title: MIDI versus SMPTE
docs.text:
This is a classic assignment question, so expect it in the exam.

MIDI SMPTE Stands for Musical Instrument Digital Interface Society of Motion Picture and Television Engineers (timing code) Purpose Exchange musical information between instruments and computers (notes, timing, instrument) Precisely synchronise audio and video with a time code Data Messages describing a performance: start of notes, intensity, instrument, channel HH:MM:SS:FF time stamps for each frame Timing role MIDI clock keeps devices in step (tempo) Frame-accurate timing for film and television Bandwidth Light; can be carried on a MIDI connection Needs more bandwidth than a MIDI connection supports Example A keyboard sending note messages to a synthesizer A film editor lining up a soundtrack with video at 24 fps

docs.title: MIDI software
docs.text:
Type Purpose Examples MIDI player Plays MIDI music Windows Media Player, the Creative MIDI player that comes with the sound card, freeware/shareware players such as Midigate and Yamaha Midplug MIDI sequencer Records, edits and plays MIDI Cakewalk Express, Home Studio, Professional; Cubasis; Encore; Voyetra MIDI Orchestrator Plus

Configuration: like audio devices, MIDI devices require a driver. Select and configure the MIDI device from the control panel.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
Name the two components of a MIDI interface.

The hardware (port, cable and electrical signalling) and the data format (messages that encode score start/end, frequency, loudness and instrument).

How many channels and instruments does the MIDI standard define?

16 channels and 128 instruments (identified by number, including noise effects).

Why does SMPTE not run over an ordinary MIDI connection?

Because SMPTE carries detailed timing information for every frame, which needs more bandwidth than a MIDI connection can support.

docs.title: Unit 2: Practice Questions
docs.text:
Unit 2Practice6 min read

Write your own answer on paper first, then click to reveal the model answer. Marks are a guide to how much detail the question deserves.

docs.title: Short answer
docs.text:
1. Differentiate sound and audio. (3 marks)

Sound is mechanical wave energy (longitudinal sound waves) that travels through a medium and causes pressure variations: the action of vibration. Audio is electrical energy (an analog or digital signal) that represents sound: the end result, the technology used to hear sounds from natural or human-made sources. A microphone's transducer converts the sound energy into a voltage.

2. Define frequency and amplitude, with units and the audible range. (4 marks)

Frequency: reciprocal of the period; the number of periods per second, in hertz. The human audible range is 20 Hz to 20 kHz. Amplitude: displacement of the air-pressure wave from its mean value; perceived as loudness; measured in decibels.

3. State the Nyquist sampling theorem and explain why CD audio uses 44.1 kHz. (3 marks)

For lossless digitization the sampling rate must be at least twice the maximum frequency. A rate of 44,100 Hz can represent frequencies up to 22,050 Hz, which covers the audible range up to 20 kHz.

4. A recording is 30 seconds of mono sound at 22.05 kHz and 8 bits. Find the file size. (3 marks)

S = R × (b/8) × C × D = 22050 × (8/8) × 1 × 30 = 661,500 bytes ≈ 646.0 KB ≈ 0.63 MB.

5. Differentiate MIDI and SMPTE with a suitable example. (5 marks)

MIDI is a standard (hardware plus data format) for exchanging musical information (notes, timing, instrument, channel) between instruments and computers. It stores instructions, not samples. SMPTE is a time code (HH:MM:SS:FF) used in film and television to precisely synchronise audio and video; it needs more bandwidth than a MIDI connection because it carries timing for each frame. Example: a keyboard sends note messages to a synthesizer over MIDI; a film editor aligns a soundtrack to video at 24 fps using SMPTE.

6. Differentiate a phone, an allophone and a morph. (3 marks)

A phone is the smallest speech unit that distinguishes one word from another (m of mat). Allophones are variants of a phone (aspirated p of pit, unaspirated p of spit). A morph is the smallest speech unit that carries meaning (consider).

7. Differentiate voiced and unvoiced sounds. (2 marks)

Voiced sounds are produced by the oscillation of the vocal cords (m, v, l) and depend strongly on the speaker. Unvoiced sounds are produced with the vocal cords open (f, s) and are relatively independent of the speaker.

8. What is an acoustic fingerprint, and what is it used for? (2 marks)

A digitally stored speech probe of a person (for example a certain statement), used to identify and verify the speaker.

docs.title: Long answer
docs.text:
9. Explain how an analog sound wave is converted to digital form, including sampling, quantization and the effect on file size. (8 marks)
  • The computer measures the amplitude at regular time intervals to give samples; an ADC does this and a DAC reverses it.
  • Sampling rate (Hz): by Nyquist, at least twice the highest frequency. CD standard 44,100 Hz represents up to 22,050 Hz.
  • Quantization: the bits per sample set the number of levels (8-bit = 256, 16-bit = 65,536, 3-bit = 8). Fewer bits give lower quality.
  • File size S = R × (b/8) × C × D. Example: 10 s stereo at 44.1 kHz and 16 bits = 1,764,000 bytes ≈ 1.68 MB. Higher rate and resolution give higher quality but bigger files; compression reduces the size.
10. Explain MIDI: purpose, interface components, messages, devices and software. (8 marks)
  • Purpose: describe music symbolically (notes, timing, instrument) so instruments from different makers can exchange information; standard from the early 1980s.
  • Components: hardware (MIDI port, cable, electrical signals) and data format (start/end of score, basic frequency, loudness, instrument; no sample values).
  • Messages: playing a key generates a message defining the start of the note and its intensity, sent to connected machines.
  • Devices: an instrument complying with both components (for example a synthesizer); 16 channels; 128 instruments (0 piano, 12 marimba, 40 violin, 73 flute).
  • Software: MIDI players and sequencers; devices need a driver configured from the control panel.
11. Explain time-dependent and frequency-dependent sound concatenation in speech generation. (6 marks)

Time-dependent: stored sound segments are pieced together as building blocks (phones, diphones, syllables, whole words). A few phones give an unlimited vocabulary; whole words give the best pronunciation. Natural-sounding but needs extensive databases and careful transitions. Frequency-dependent: e.g. formant synthesis; formants are frequency maxima in the spectrum; mathematical vocal-tract models control formant frequency and amplitude. Flexible and low storage, but harder to make natural.

12. Describe speech recognition with a block diagram. (8 marks)

Definition: converting an acoustic signal from a microphone or telephone into a set of words (written text). It depends on speaker (dependent/independent), speech (discrete words/continuous), vocabulary (small/large) and environment (quiet/noisy). Principle: extract characteristics to reduce data: speech analysis (parameter and property extraction) feeds pattern recognition (comparison with reference storage and a decision) to give recognised speech. Steps: acoustic and phonetic analysis (sound patterns, word models) → syntactical analysis (syntax) → semantic analysis (semantics) → understood speech.

13. Explain the principles of speech transmission. (6 marks)

PCM: digitises the waveform, ignores speech-specific properties, favours accurate representation over data reduction. Source encoding: uses signal properties (silence suppression, parametric systems such as the channel vocoder); chain A/D → speech analysis → coded signal → reconstruction → D/A. Recognition/synthesis: recognition at the sender, synthesis at the receiver, and only the characteristics of the speech elements are transmitted.

docs.title: Multiple choice
docs.text:
14. The human audible range is
  • A. 0 to 20 Hz
  • B. 20 Hz to 20 kHz
  • C. 20 kHz to 1 GHz
  • D. 1 GHz to 10 THz

Answer: B. A is infrasound, C ultrasound, D hypersound.

15. A CD sampling rate of 44,100 Hz can represent frequencies up to
  • A. 44,100 Hz
  • B. 22,050 Hz
  • C. 88,200 Hz
  • D. 16,000 Hz

Answer: B. By the Nyquist theorem the maximum frequency is half the sampling rate.

16. How many levels does 16-bit quantization give?
  • A. 256
  • B. 4,096
  • C. 65,536
  • D. 16

Answer: C. 2¹⁶ = 65,536. 256 is 8-bit.

17. In the file-size formula S = R × (b/8) × C × D, what does C stand for?
  • A. Compression ratio
  • B. Number of channels
  • C. Clock rate
  • D. Codec

Answer: B. C is the number of channels (1 = mono, 2 = stereo).

18. How many channels does the MIDI standard specify?
  • A. 8
  • B. 16
  • C. 64
  • D. 128

Answer: B. 16 channels. 128 is the number of instruments.

19. SMPTE time code is expressed as
  • A. HH:MM:SS:FF
  • B. DD:MM:YYYY
  • C. kbps:fps
  • D. Hz:dB

Answer: A. Hours, minutes, seconds and frames.

20. Which technique builds speech from formants?
  • A. Time-dependent sound concatenation
  • B. Frequency-dependent sound concatenation
  • C. Pulse code modulation
  • D. Silence suppression

Answer: B. Formants are frequency maxima, so formant synthesis is frequency-dependent.

21. Which of these is a lossless audio format?
  • A. MP3
  • B. AAC
  • C. FLAC
  • D. WMA

Answer: C. MP3, AAC and WMA are lossy.

22. In the recognition/synthesis method of speech transmission, recognition takes place
  • A. At the receiver
  • B. At the sender
  • C. On the network
  • D. Nowhere; only synthesis is used

Answer: B. Recognition at the sender, synthesis at the receiver, and only the characteristics of the speech elements are transmitted.
