docs.title: Basic Sound Concepts
docs.text: Unit 2Notes3 min read

docs.title: What is sound?
docs.text:
Sound is the physical phenomenon produced by the vibration of matter.

When matter vibrates, pressure variations are created in the surrounding air. This alternation of high and low pressure travels through the air in a wave-like motion. When the wave reaches the human ear, a sound is heard.

docs.title: Waveform and period
docs.text:
• The pattern of the oscillation is called a waveform.
  • The waveform repeats the same shape at regular intervals. One such interval is called a period.
  • Natural sound waves are never perfectly smooth or uniformly periodic.

A typical diagram shows air pressure plotted against time as a smooth wave: the vertical distance from the middle line to a peak is the amplitude, and the horizontal distance of one full repeat is one period.

docs.title: Periodic and non-periodic sound
docs.text: Examples Periodic sound Musical instruments, vowel sounds, whistling wind, bird songs Non-periodic sound Unpitched percussion instruments, coughs, sneezes, rushing water, consonants such as "t", "f" and "s"

docs.title: Frequency
docs.text:
The frequency of a sound is the reciprocal of the period. It is the number of periods in one second, measured in hertz (Hz) or cycles per second (cps).

\[\text{frequency} = \frac{1}{\text{period}} \qquad 1\ \text{kHz} = 1000\ \text{Hz}\]

docs.title: Frequency ranges
docs.text:
Range Frequencies Infrasound 0 – 20 Hz Human audible sound 20 Hz – 20 kHz Ultrasound 20 kHz – 1 GHz Hypersound 1 GHz – 10 THz

Human audible sound is also called audio or acoustic signals (waves). Speech is an acoustic signal produced by humans.

Exam tip

Learn the four ranges in order, with the numbers. The audible range (20 Hz to 20 kHz) is the one used in every later calculation, including the Nyquist theorem.

docs.title: Amplitude
docs.text:
A sound has a property called amplitude, which humans perceive subjectively as loudness or volume. The amplitude is the measure of the displacement of the air pressure wave from its mean (quiescent or idle) value. The greater the amplitude, the louder the sound.

Loudness is measured in decibels (dB):

Level Meaning 0 dB Essentially no sound heard 35 dB Quiet home 70 dB Noisy street 120 dB Discomfort Property Physical meaning What we perceive Frequency Periods per second (Hz) Pitch Amplitude Displacement from the mean pressure Loudness (volume)

Extra

Amplitude is linked amplitude to loudness. The usual pairing for frequency is pitch (higher frequency, higher note); pitch is mentioned only later, in the speech section.

docs.title: Sound versus audio
docs.text:
Sound Audio Form of energy Mechanical wave energy (longitudinal sound waves) Electrical energy (analog or digital signals) that represents sound What it is Vibrations through a material; the action The end result: the technology to hear sounds from natural or human-made sources Nature A continuous wave travelling through air, measured as the pressure level at a point A signal made from that wave

A microphone is the bridge: the sound field moves its surface according to the varying pressure, and a transducer converts this energy into a voltage level (electrical energy).

Exam tip

"Differentiate sound and audio" is a classic short question. Write both rows: mechanical wave energy versus electrical signal, and action versus end result.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
Define frequency and give the audible range.

Frequency is the reciprocal of the period: the number of periods per second, measured in hertz. The human audible range is 20 Hz to 20 kHz.

What does amplitude determine, and how is it measured?

Amplitude is the displacement of the air pressure wave from its mean value. Humans perceive it as loudness and it is measured in decibels.

Is a vowel sound periodic or non-periodic? And a consonant such as 's'?

A vowel sound is periodic. Consonants such as "t", "f" and "s" are non-periodic.

docs.title: Speech Analysis
docs.text:
Unit 2Notes3 min read

Speech analysis (speech input) asks three questions about a spoken signal. It is often drawn as a tree: Speech analysis splits into Who? (verification and identification), What? (recognition and understanding) and How?.

flowchart TB
    SA["Speech analysis"] --> W["Who?"]
    SA --> WH["What?"]
    SA --> H["How?"]
    W --> V["Verification"]
    W --> I["Identification"]
    WH --> R["Recognition"]
    WH --> U["Understanding"]

docs.title: Who is speaking?
docs.text:
Human speech has characteristics that are determined by the speaker. Speech analysis can therefore recognise a speaker for identification and verification.

  • The computer identifies and verifies the speaker using an acoustic fingerprint.
  • An acoustic fingerprint is a digitally stored speech probe of a person (for example, a certain statement).

docs.title: What has been said?
docs.text:
This task analyses what was said: to recognise and understand the speech signal itself. A corresponding text is generated from the speech sequence. Applications:

  • A speech-controlled typewriter
  • A translation system
  • Part of a workplace for the handicapped

docs.title: How was it said?
docs.text:
This area researches the speech pattern of a statement: how a certain sentence was said. A spoken sentence sounds different if a person is angry or calm.

Question Task Example Who? Identification and verification of the speaker, using an acoustic fingerprint Voice-based access What? Recognition and understanding of the content Speech-controlled typewriter, translation How? The manner of speaking (patterns in the voice) Angry versus calm

docs.title: Speech recognition
docs.text:
Speech recognition is the process of converting an acoustic signal, captured by a microphone or a telephone, to a set of words (that is, spoken language to written text or a similar form). It is the foundation of human-computer interaction using speech.

Recognition systems differ along four contexts:

Context Options The speaker Speaker-dependent or speaker-independent The speech Discrete words or continuous speech The vocabulary Small or large The environment Quiet or noisy

docs.title: The recognition principle (Figure 3-13)
docs.text:
The principle is "extract characteristics to reduce data." A typical diagram shows:

  1. Speech analysis (on a special chip): parameters, response and property extraction from the speech signal.
  2. Pattern recognition (on the main processor): comparison with reference material and a decision.
  3. Reference storage: the properties of the learned material, consulted during comparison.

The output is the recognised speech.

flowchart LR
    S["Speech"] --> A["Speech analysis (special chip): extract parameters"]
    A --> P["Pattern recognition (main processor): compare and decide"]
    R["Reference storage: learned material"] <--> P
    P --> O["Recognised speech"]

docs.title: The recognition steps (Figure 3-14)
docs.text:
Applying the principle gives three analysis stages, each using a knowledge source:

Stage Knowledge used Acoustic and phonetic analysis Sound patterns and word models Syntactical analysis Syntax Semantic analysis Semantics

The output of the last stage is understood speech. In the usual diagram each stage can feed back to the previous one.

Exam tip

"Explain speech recognition" is a likely long question. Give the definition, the four contexts, and the three-stage diagram (acoustic/phonetic → syntactical → semantic), each labelled with its knowledge source.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
What is an acoustic fingerprint?

A digitally stored speech probe of a person (for example a certain statement), used to identify or verify who is speaking.

State the three questions of speech analysis.

Who is speaking (identification and verification), what was said (recognition and understanding) and how it was said (for example angry or calm).

Name the three stages of recognition and the knowledge each uses.

Acoustic and phonetic analysis (sound patterns, word models), syntactical analysis (syntax), semantic analysis (semantics).

docs.title: Speech Generation
docs.text: Unit 2Notes3 min read

docs.title: About speech
docs.text:
Speech is the vocalised form of human communication. It can be perceived, understood and generated by humans and also by machines.

  • A human adjusts very efficiently to different speakers and their speech habits.
  • The brain can recognise the very fine line between speech and noise.
  • The human speech signal contains a subjective lowest spectral component called the pitch, which is not proportional to frequency.

Speech generation is the computer-generated simulation of human speech. Generated speech must be understandable and must sound natural.

docs.title: Basic notions
docs.text:
Term Definition Example Fundamental frequency The lowest periodic spectral component of the speech signal; present in a voiced sound Phone The smallest speech unit that distinguishes one utterance or word from another in a language The m of mat and the b of bat Allophones Variants of a phone The aspirated p of pit and the unaspirated p of spit are allophones of the English phoneme p Morph The smallest speech unit that carries a meaning itself consider is a morph; reconsideration is not Voiced sound Generated by the oscillation of the vocal cords; depends strongly on each speaker m, v, l Unvoiced sound Generated with the vocal cords open; relatively independent of the speaker f, s

Exam tip

Know the phone versus morph contrast: a phone is the smallest unit of sound; a morph is the smallest unit of meaning. Know voiced versus unvoiced with one example each.

docs.title: Reproduced speech output: two methods
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    A["Speech output (generation)"] --> B["Time-dependent sound concatenation"]
    A --> C["Frequency-dependent sound concatenation"]
    B --> B1["Piece together stored sound segments: phones, diphones, syllables, whole words"]
    C --> C1["Formant synthesis: model the vocal tract and control formant frequencies"]

docs.title: Time-dependent sound concatenation
docs.text:
Pre-recorded or pre-synthesised sound segments are pieced together based on their timing. Individual speech units are composed like building blocks, and the composition can happen at different levels.

  1. Phones. With just a few phones it is possible to create an unlimited vocabulary.
  2. Diphones. Two phones form a diphone. For example, the word crumb is built from an ordered sequence of diphones.
  3. Syllables. To make the transition problem easier, syllables can be created, and speech is generated from a set of syllables (for example crumb as one syllable sound).
  4. Whole words. The best pronunciation of a word comes from storing the whole word. This leads to synthesis of the whole speech sequence.

Assessment: often used in high-quality text-to-speech (TTS) systems for its naturalness, but it needs extensive databases and careful management of transitions.

docs.title: Frequency-dependent sound concatenation
docs.text:
Speech is generated by manipulating the frequency components of sound, for example through formant synthesis.

  • Formants are frequency maxima in the spectrum of the speech signal.
  • Formant synthesis uses mathematical models of the vocal tract to generate speech sounds by controlling the frequency and amplitude of the formants (resonant frequencies).

Assessment: offers more flexibility and needs less storage, but can struggle to sound natural.

Time-dependent concatenation Frequency-dependent concatenation Idea Join stored sound segments Generate speech from formant models Units Phones, diphones, syllables, words Formants (frequency maxima) Strength Natural sound Flexible, little storage Weakness Large databases; transitions between units Hard to make natural-sounding

docs.title: Speech synthesis: the two-step process
docs.text:
Speech synthesis transforms an existing text into an acoustic signal. A typical diagram shows the flow: Text → Transcription (with a Dictionary) → Sound script → Synthesis (with Sound transfer) → Speech.

flowchart LR
    T["Text"] --> TR["Transcription"]
    D["Dictionary"] <--> TR
    TR -->|"Sound script"| SY["Synthesis"]
    ST["Sound transfer"] --> SY
    SY --> SP["Speech"]

Step 1: Transcription. The text is translated into a sound script using a dictionary. If the user notices a deficiency in the transcription, they can improve the pronunciation manually.

Step 2: Synthesis. The sound script is translated into a speech signal. Time-dependent or frequency-dependent concatenation can follow.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
Differentiate a phone and a morph.

A phone is the smallest unit of speech sound that distinguishes one word from another (the m of mat). A morph is the smallest unit that carries meaning (consider).

What are formants, and which generation method uses them?

Formants are frequency maxima in the spectrum of the speech signal. Frequency-dependent sound concatenation (formant synthesis) uses mathematical models of the vocal tract to control them.

Describe the two steps of speech synthesis.

Transcription: text is converted to a sound script using a dictionary. Synthesis: the sound script is converted to a speech signal, using time-dependent or frequency-dependent concatenation.

docs.title: Speech Transmission
docs.text:
Unit 2Notes2 min read

Speech transmission is the field of highly efficient encoding of speech signals so they can be sent at a low data rate while keeping noticeable quality loss to a minimum.

There are three principles:

  1. Pulse Code Modulation (PCM)
  2. Source coding
  3. Recognition and synthesis methods

docs.title: 1. Pulse Code Modulation (PCM)
docs.text:
• Signal-form encoding does not consider speech-specific properties or parameters. The techniques are simply expected to encode audio signals efficiently.
  • A straightforward technique for digitising an analog signal (waveform) is PCM.
  • PCM prioritises the accurate representation of the audio signal over data reduction.

docs.title: 2. Source encoding
docs.text:
An alternative method: some transformations depend on the original signal type. An audio signal has certain characteristics that can be exploited in compression.

  • Suppressing silence in speech sequences is a typical example. It depends entirely on the meaning (semantics) of the signal.
  • Parametric systems use source encoding. They use speech-specific characteristics to reduce data, for example the channel vocoder.

A typical diagram shows the components of a transmission system using source encoding:

flowchart TB
    A["Analog speech signal"] --> AD["A/D"]
    AD --> SA["Speech analysis"]
    SA -->|"Coded speech signal"| RC["Reconstruction"]
    RC --> DA["D/A"]
    DA --> O["Analog speech signal"]

docs.title: 3. Recognition / synthesis method
docs.text:
• Speech analysis (recognition) takes place on the sender side of the transmission system.
  • Speech synthesis (generation) takes place on the receiver side.
  • Only the characteristics of the speech elements are transmitted, not the waveform.

docs.title: Comparing the three principles
docs.text:
PCM Source encoding Recognition / synthesis Uses speech-specific properties? No (signal-form encoding) Yes (e.g. silence suppression, channel vocoder) Yes, fully What is sent Digitised waveform samples Coded (analysed) speech parameters Only the characteristics of the speech elements Priority Accurate representation Reduce data using signal semantics Lowest data rate Sender / receiver Digitise / reconstruct Analyse / reconstruct Recognise (sender) / synthesise (receiver)

Exam tip

A clean three-row table like this earns full marks for "Explain the principles of speech transmission". Put one example in each row: PCM (digitising the waveform), silence suppression (source encoding), recognise-then-synthesise (only characteristics sent).

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
What does PCM prioritise and what does it ignore?

It prioritises an accurate representation of the audio signal over data reduction, and it ignores speech-specific properties (it is signal-form encoding).

Give one example of source encoding.

Suppression of silence in speech sequences, or a channel vocoder (a parametric system).

In the recognition/synthesis method, which side performs recognition?

The sender. The receiver performs synthesis, so only the characteristics of the speech elements travel over the channel.

docs.title: Unit 3: Image and Graphics
docs.text:
4 hours · weeks 3–4 · syllabus items 3.1 and 3.2

Sound was one stream of numbers over time. An image is a grid of numbers over space. This unit explains how a picture is stored (pixels, bitmaps, colour depth), how it differs from a graphic (a set of drawing instructions), how images are generated (synthesis), understood (analysis and recognition) and sent over a network.

Open the class slides

docs.title: What you must master
docs.text:
1. Distinguish an image from a graphic, and a bitmap from graphics primitives.
  2. Calculate the storage of a bitmap from its width, height and bits per pixel.
  3. Explain the capturing, storage and graphics formats, and name common file formats.
  4. Describe image synthesis, the three-part interactive graphics framework, raster display hardware and dithering.
  5. Explain image analysis and the steps of image recognition.
  6. Describe the three ways of transmitting an image (raw, compressed, symbolic) and calculate raw image size.

docs.title: Syllabus coverage
docs.text: Syllabus item Where to read it Coverage 3.1 Basic concept: representation Image and Graphics Basics Full 3.1 Image format, graphics format Image and Graphics Formats Full 3.2 Synthesis Image Synthesis and Graphics Systems Full 3.2 Analysis Image Analysis and Recognition Full 3.2 Transmission Image Transmission Full

docs.title: Reading order
docs.text:
1. Image and Graphics Basics
  2. Image and Graphics Formats
  3. Image Synthesis and Graphics Systems
  4. Image Analysis and Recognition
  5. Image Transmission
  6. Practice Questions

docs.title: What to expect in the exam
docs.text:
These weights are estimates based on how much space each topic usually gets. They are not from a past paper.

Most likely questions

  • Image versus graphics (a comparison table).
  • Bitmap size calculations (worked examples appear in these notes).
  • Image synthesis and analysis: definitions, applications, and the three-component graphics framework.
  • Dithering and the 125 colours calculation.
  • Image recognition steps, and the three image transmission formats with the raw-size formula.

docs.title: Before Next Class
docs.text:
• Redo the three size examples (16×16, 100×100, 960×640) without looking.
  • Learn the image-versus-graphics table.
  • List the recognition steps in order, with one line each.
  • Skim the Unit 4 overview.

docs.title: Image and Graphics Formats
docs.text:
Unit 3Notes3 min read

Two kinds of two distinct kinds of image format: the format in which the image is created during digitising (capturing format), and the format in which images are stored and often transmitted (storage format). Graphics formats are a separate case.

docs.title: Image capturing format
docs.text:
The format is specified by two main parameters:

  1. Spatial resolution, indicated in pixels (pixels × pixels).
  2. Colour encoding, specified by bits per pixel.

The values of both depend on the hardware and software used to input and output images.

  • Example: a SPARCstation captures images at 320 × 240.
  • Colour encoding may be 1 bit, 8 bits or 24 bits.

docs.title: Image storage format
docs.text:
The image is stored as a two-dimensional matrix in which each value corresponds to the data for one pixel.

  • In bitmaps the values are binary numbers.
  • In colour images it is good to store RGB triples (red, green and blue components).
  • Example: a 640 × 480, 24-bit colour image needs 900 KB (921,600 bytes).

docs.title: File formats to know
docs.text:
Format Extension(s) Microsoft Windows DIB .bmp, .dib, .rle Microsoft Palette .pal AutoCAD format 2D .dxf JPEG (Joint Photographic/Picture Experts Group) .jpg Windows Metafile .wmf Portable Network Graphics .png CompuServe GIF (Graphics Interchange Format) .gif Apple Macintosh .pict, .pic, .pct

Other formats mentioned in the text: X11 bitmap, PostScript, TIFF (Tagged Image File Format), and IRIS.

docs.title: Graphics format
docs.text:
Graphics image formats are not specified by pixels. They are specified through graphics primitives and their attributes.

Examples Graphics primitives Lines, rectangles, circles, ellipses, text strings (2D); polyhedron (3D) Graphics attributes Line style, line width, colour

Primitives and attributes are a higher-level description of the image. At some point in processing, for example when the computer displays the image, this higher level must be mapped to a lower level (pixels).

Points Advantages Reduces the data volume stored for each image; allows simpler image manipulation Disadvantage An additional conversion step from primitives and attributes to the pixel representation

docs.title: Graphics packages
docs.text: Package Note SRGP (Simple Raster Graphics Package) Includes the primitives-to-bitmap conversion (one-way conversion to bit/pixmap) PHIGS (Programmer's Hierarchical Interactive Graphics System) A graphics standard of this type GKS (Graphical Kernel System) A graphics standard of this type; image representation only in pixmap

docs.title: Comparison of the three formats
docs.text:
Capturing format Storage format Graphics format Described by Spatial resolution + bits per pixel 2D matrix of pixel values Primitives + attributes When it matters While digitising an image When saving or sending an image When describing an image symbolically Depends on Input/output hardware and software File format chosen Graphics package Example 320 × 240, 8 bits GIF, JPEG, TIFF, PNG SRGP, PHIGS, GKS

Exam tip

A common question is "Explain image formats". Cover capturing (two parameters), storage (2D matrix, RGB triples, file formats) and graphics (primitives, attributes, advantage and disadvantage).

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
Which two parameters specify an image capturing format?

Spatial resolution in pixels and colour encoding in bits per pixel.

Give one advantage and one disadvantage of graphics primitives.

Advantage: less data to store and simpler manipulation. Disadvantage: an extra conversion step from primitives and attributes to pixels.

Name four image file formats with their extensions.

For example GIF (.gif), JPEG (.jpg), PNG (.png), Windows DIB (.bmp); also TIFF, DXF (.dxf) and PICT (.pict).

docs.title: Image Analysis and Recognition
docs.text: Unit 3Notes4 min read

docs.title: Image analysis
docs.text:
Image analysis is concerned with techniques for extracting descriptions of objects from images. In some textbooks' terms, image-processing algorithms alter an input image to create a new image, or extract image descriptions (shape, position, orientation) for higher-level analysis.

Analysis techniques include:

  • Computation of perceived brightness and colour.
  • Partial or complete recovery of 3D data in a scene.
  • Location of discontinuities that correspond to objects in the scene.
  • Characterisation of the properties of uniform regions in the image.

It may also deal with calculating and comparing intensity, hue and saturation, the centroid, identifying noise, detecting patterns, or recognising the image itself.

docs.title: Analysis versus recognition
docs.text: Image recognition Image analysis Techniques Relies heavily on classification models A broader range: segmentation, feature extraction, statistical analysis Purpose Identifying and categorising Detailed examination and understanding of images

docs.title: Applications of image analysis
docs.text:
• Aerial surveillance photographs
  • Slow-scan images of the moon or planets from space probes
  • Television images from an industrial robot's visual sensor
  • X-ray images and CAT (computerised axial tomography) scans

docs.title: Areas of image processing
docs.text:
Area What it does Example Image enhancement Improves quality by removing noise or enhancing contrast X-ray images, CAT scans Pattern detection and recognition Detects and classifies standard patterns and finds distortions from the patterns OCR (optical character recognition) Scene analysis Describes what is in a scene Computer vision Recognises and reconstructs 3D models of a scene from several 2D images A robot sensing the size, shape, position and colour of objects

Static versus dynamic recognition (OCR)

Recognising characters while they are being written is easier than recognising scanned characters, because a dynamic recogniser records the sequence, direction, speed and pressure of each stroke.

docs.title: Image recognition
docs.text:
To fully recognise an object in an image means knowing that there is agreement between the sensory projections and the observed image. How the object appears is given by the spatial configuration of the pixel values, so the observed configuration must agree with the expected one.

This requires two capabilities:

  1. Infer the object's position and orientation from the spatial configuration. That means working out which pixels belong to the object, and distinguishing features such as special markings, curves and lines.
  2. Confirm the inference is correct by matching distinguishing image features with the corresponding object features.

The difficulty of recognition depends on the kind of object, the background, the imaging sensor and similar factors. A simple corner extraction can identify some images.

docs.title: Steps of image recognition
docs.text:
Exam tip

This is a likely long question. Different books give slightly different lists: some give six steps (including Grouping), some five (no grouping). Learn the six and write them in this order. Mention grouping with one line.

flowchart LR
    A["1 Formatting"] --> B["2 Conditioning"]
    B --> C["3 Labeling"]
    C --> D["4 Grouping"]
    D --> E["5 Extracting"]
    E --> F["6 Matching"]
# Step What happens 1 Formatting Capture the image from a camera and bring it into digital form: a pixel representation. 2 Conditioning Preprocess the data to make it suitable for recognition. Suppress noise and background, which hide informative patterns, and highlight the interesting parts. Tasks: noise reduction, image enhancement, normalisation, feature extraction. 3 Labeling Assign labels to the structure. In other treatments: analyse adjacent pixels to find structure such as edges (edge detection finds continuous adjacent pixels that differ greatly in intensity or colour; a threshold filters out insignificant edges) and corners; edges and corners are labelled. In the main slides: assign semantic labels or categories to objects or patterns. 4 Grouping Organise similar objects or patterns into groups, for example with clustering to form coherent regions. (Unit 3 only.) 5 Extracting Compute a list of properties for each group of pixels: centroid, area, orientation, spatial moments, gray-tone moments, number of holes, average curvature. It also describes the topological relationship between groups. Techniques: edge detection, texture analysis, shape analysis. 6 Matching Compare each object in the image with previously stored models or templates and determine the best match. Uses similarity measures, template matching or classifiers.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
Differentiate image analysis and image recognition.

Recognition identifies and categorises, relying on classification models. Analysis is a broader, detailed examination using segmentation, feature extraction and statistical analysis.

Why is dynamic character recognition easier than scanned-character recognition?

Because a dynamic recogniser records the sequence, direction, speed and pressure of each stroke as it is written.

List the steps of image recognition in order.

Formatting, conditioning, labeling, grouping, extracting, matching.

docs.title: Image and Graphics Basics
docs.text: Unit 3Notes4 min read

docs.title: What is an image?
docs.text:
An image is a spatial representation of an object: a two-dimensional or three-dimensional scene, or another image. Abstractly, an image is a continuous function defining a rectangular region of a plane.

Where it appears Form of the image Recorded image Photograph, analog video signal, or digital format Computer vision Video image, digital image or picture Computer graphics Digital image Multimedia All of the above

docs.title: The digital image
docs.text:
A digital image is a matrix of numeric values given by the function I(r, c), where r and c are the row and column of a point.

  • The point is called a pixel.
  • I(r, c) is the intensity value (gray level) at that point.
  • Gray scale for a monochrome picture: 0 and 1. For an 8-bit image: 0 to 255.
  • The number of pixels is the resolution.

docs.title: Image versus graphics
docs.text:
Exam tip

This comparison is the most likely short question in the unit. Learn all four rows.

Graphics Image How it is made Created in a graphics application and represented internally as an assemblage of objects such as lines, curves or circles Comes from the real world or is virtual; captured from an analog signal by a scanner or video camera, or created with software tools Semantics The representation is aware of semantics Ignores semantic content Editing Objects can be individually deleted, added, moved or modified later Object-based editing is not possible, but tools exist for enhancing and retouching bitmap images Storage Stores an abstract definition (small) Stores a bitmap: much more storage Display The definition must be processed first to produce a bitmap No processing needed before display
  • The smallest addressable image element is a pixel.
  • The array of pixels is a bitmap.
  • Drawback of bitmaps: they need much more storage than graphics.
  • Advantage of bitmaps: no processing before display.

docs.title: Bitmaps
docs.text: A bitmap with 1 bit per pixel is a monochrome image (this is what very early computers could manage): each pixel is either 0 (off) or 1 (on).

docs.title: Worked example 1: a 16 × 16 bitmap
docs.text:
A typical diagram shows a black cat drawn on a 16 × 16 grid, with the 0s and 1s printed beside it.

Step Working Pixels 16 × 16 = 256 pixels Bits per pixel 1 bit Total bits 256 bits In bytes 256 / 8 = 32 bytes

docs.title: Bitmap resolution
docs.text: Image resolution is a measure of pixel density, given in dots per inch (dpi). Smaller pixels fit more on the screen, which means a higher pixel density. A resolution of 300 dpi means 300 pixels (dots) packed into each inch.

docs.title: Worked example 3: a 100 × 100 bitmap
docs.text: Step Working Pixels 100 × 100 = 10,000 Bits 10,000 bits (1 bit per pixel) Bytes 10,000 / 8 = 1,250 bytes Kilobytes 1,250 / 1,024 = 1.22 KB

docs.title: Colour bitmaps
docs.text:
To show colour you need more bits per pixel. The number of colours is 2 raised to the bits per pixel.

Bits per pixel Colours Name 1 2 Monochrome 4 16 8 2⁸ = 256 Pseudo colour (one byte per pixel) 24 2²⁴ = 16,777,216 True colour (three bytes per pixel)

In 24-bit colour each byte holds the intensity of one primary colour: Red, Green and Blue, each with 256 levels (256 × 256 × 256 colours).

The depth of an image is the number of bits used to represent each pixel.

8-bit (pseudo colour) 24-bit (true colour) Bytes per pixel 1 3 Colours 256 256 × 256 × 256 640 × 480 image needs 307.2 KB 921.6 KB

docs.title: The general formula
docs.text:
\[\text{Size (bits)} = \text{width} \times \text{height} \times \text{bits per pixel} \qquad \text{Size (bytes)} = \frac{\text{width} \times \text{height} \times \text{bits per pixel}}{8}\]

KB can mean two things

A 640 × 480 24-bit image is sometimes quoted as 921.6 KB (dividing by 1000) and sometimes as 900K (dividing by 1024). Both come from 640 × 480 × 3 = 921,600 bytes. In the exam, state the byte count first, then give the KB value and say which you divided by.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
Differentiate an image and a graphic in two points.

A graphic is stored as objects (lines, curves, circles) with semantics, so objects can be edited individually and the file is small but needs processing before display. An image is a bitmap of pixels that ignores semantics, needs more storage, and is displayed without processing.

How many bytes are needed for a 16 × 16 monochrome bitmap?

16 × 16 = 256 pixels at 1 bit each = 256 bits = 32 bytes.

Why does a 24-bit image give 16,777,216 colours?

24 bits per pixel gives 2²⁴ = 16,777,216 combinations: 8 bits each for red, green and blue, each with 256 levels.

docs.title: Image Transmission
docs.text:
Unit 3Notes2 min read

Image transmission is the sending of digital images through computer networks.

docs.title: Requirements on the network
docs.text:
Requirement Why The network must handle bursty data Image transmission is bursty because of the large size of images Transport must be reliable A lost part of an image damages the picture Time dependence is not dominant Unlike audio and video, an image has no real-time deadline

Compare with audio and video

An image is a discrete medium (no time component), so its transmission needs reliable, bursty transport rather than the steady, on-time delivery that continuous media need. This links back to Media Concepts.

docs.title: Three ways to send an image
docs.text:
The image size depends on the representation format used for transmission.

flowchart TB
    I["Image transmission formats"] --> R["Raw image data"]
    I --> C["Compressed image data"]
    I --> S["Symbolic image data"]

docs.title: 1. Raw image data transmission
docs.text:
The image is generated by a video digitiser and transmitted in its digital format.

\[\text{Size} = \text{Spatial resolution} \times \text{Pixel quantization}\]

Example: a 640 × 480 image with 8 bits per pixel:

\[640 \times 480 \times 8 = 2{,}457{,}600 \text{ bits} = 307{,}200 \text{ bytes}\]

docs.title: 2. Compressed image data transmission
docs.text:
The image is generated by a video digitiser and compressed before transmission.

  • Methods such as JPEG or MPEG are used.
  • The reduction in size depends on the compression method and compression rate.

docs.title: 3. Symbolic image data transmission
docs.text:
The image is represented by symbolic data: image primitives (for example 2D or 3D geometric representation), attributes and other control information.

  • This representation is used in computer graphics.
  • The image size equals the size of the structure that carries the symbolic information.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text:
Raw Compressed Symbolic What is sent Every pixel Compressed pixel data Primitives, attributes, control information Size depends on Resolution × pixel quantization Compression method and rate Size of the structure Typical use Video digitiser output JPEG, MPEG Computer graphics Relative size Largest Much smaller Usually smallest

Extra

The "relative size" row is a typical ordering, not a rule: a very complex drawing could produce a symbolic description larger than a compressed small photo. Only states how each size is determined.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
Why is image transmission 'bursty' and why is timing not critical?

Images are large, so they are sent as bursts of data. An image has no time component, so unlike audio and video it does not need steady, on-time delivery. It does need reliable transport.

Calculate the raw size of a 640 × 480 image at 8 bits per pixel.

640 × 480 × 8 = 2,457,600 bits = 307,200 bytes.

When is symbolic image transmission used?

In computer graphics, where the image is represented by primitives, attributes and control information, and its size equals the size of that structure.

docs.title: Unit 3: Practice Questions
docs.text:
Unit 3Practice6 min read

Write your own answer on paper first, then click to reveal the model answer. Marks are a guide to how much detail the question deserves.

docs.title: Short answer
docs.text:
1. Differentiate an image and a graphic. (4 marks)
  • Graphic: created in a graphics application; internally an assemblage of objects (lines, curves, circles); aware of semantics; objects can be individually deleted, added, moved or modified; small storage but the abstract definition must be processed to produce a bitmap before display.
  • Image: from the real world or virtual (scanner, video camera, software); a bitmap of pixels that ignores semantics; no object-based editing (only enhancing and retouching); much more storage but no processing before display.
2. Calculate the storage needed for a 64 × 64 monochrome bitmap. (2 marks)

64 × 64 = 4,096 pixels × 1 bit = 4,096 bits = 512 bytes.

3. Calculate the size of a 800 × 600 true-colour (24-bit) image. (3 marks)

800 × 600 = 480,000 pixels × 3 bytes = 1,440,000 bytes = 1,406.25 KB ≈ 1.37 MB.

4. Find the size of a 1024 × 768 image at 8 bits per pixel. (3 marks)

1024 × 768 = 786,432 pixels × 1 byte = 786,432 bytes = 768 KB = 0.75 MB.

5. Why does a 24-bit image support 16,777,216 colours? (2 marks)

24 bits per pixel give 2²⁴ = 16,777,216 combinations: 8 bits each for red, green and blue, each primary having 256 levels (256 × 256 × 256).

6. Define image synthesis and give three applications. (4 marks)

Image synthesis is the generation of images of real or imaginary objects. It is part of all computer user interfaces and indispensable for visualising 2D, 3D and higher-dimensional objects. Applications: user interface (point-and-click, menu-driven), office automation and electronic publishing (desktop publishing, hypermedia), simulation and animation for scientific visualisation and entertainment (fluid-flow models, cartoons, flying logos).

7. Differentiate motion dynamics and update dynamics with examples. (3 marks)

Motion dynamics: objects move or are activated relative to a static observer (or the environment moves), e.g. a flight simulator. Update dynamics: the shape, colour or other properties of objects actually change, e.g. deformation of an in-flight aeroplane structure.

8. What is dithering and why is it useful? (4 marks)

Dithering produces shades of gray or tints of colour on output devices (monitors, some printers) using fewer colours. It exploits the eye's spatial integration: from a distance the eye averages fine detail and records overall intensity. It is also called halftoning; the shades are halftones.

9. A 2 × 2 dither matrix is used for each of the red, green and blue channels. How many colours can be shown? (2 marks)

A 2 × 2 matrix gives 5 intensity levels per channel (0 to 4 dots lit). 5 × 5 × 5 = 125 colours.

10. Differentiate image analysis and image recognition. (3 marks)

Recognition identifies and categorises, relying heavily on classification models. Analysis is a broader, detailed examination using segmentation, feature extraction and statistical analysis.

11. State three network requirements for image transmission. (3 marks)

The network must accommodate bursty data (large images); transport should be reliable; time dependence is not dominant, unlike audio and video.

docs.title: Long answer
docs.text:
12. Explain the framework of an interactive graphics system. (8 marks)

Three software components (plus hardware):

  1. Application model: the data or objects to be pictured (descriptions of primitives, attributes and connectivity), stored in an application database, application-specific and independent of any display system.
  2. Application program: converts the model into graphics-system commands in two steps: extract the portions to be viewed (selection or query), then convert the geometry to the proper format; it sends a series of graphics output commands.
  3. Graphics system: the intermediary between program and display hardware that actually produces the picture, performing output transformations (model to view) and input transformations (user actions to application inputs).
  4. Graphics hardware: input devices (mouse, tablet, touch panel, trackball, data glove) and a raster display.
13. Explain the working of a raster display. (6 marks)

A CRT has rows of phosphor dots that glow when hit by electrons from the electron gun. Picture information is held in the refresh buffer. The video controller reads the buffer and turns the beam on and off, one row at a time, top to bottom; after each row the beam returns to the start of the next row (horizontal retrace). A display controller interprets output commands; in a PC it is software in a graphics library and the refresh buffer is part of CPU memory.

14. Explain the steps of image recognition. (8 marks)

Formatting (capture and digitise); conditioning (suppress noise and background, highlight informative patterns); labeling (find structure such as edges and corners by edge detection with a threshold; label them); grouping (cluster similar patterns into coherent regions); extracting (compute properties of each group: centroid, area, orientation, moments, holes, curvature, and relationships between groups); matching (compare each object with stored models or templates and pick the best match).

15. Explain the three formats for image transmission. (6 marks)

Raw: transmitted in digital form from the video digitiser; size = spatial resolution × pixel quantization (e.g. 640 × 480 × 8 = 2,457,600 bits = 307,200 bytes). Compressed: compressed (JPEG, MPEG) before transmission; size depends on method and rate. Symbolic: primitives, attributes and control information, as in computer graphics; size equals the structure carrying the symbols.

docs.title: Multiple choice
docs.text:
16. Which is true of a bitmap compared with graphics?
  • A. It needs less storage
  • B. It needs no processing before display
  • C. Its objects can be individually moved
  • D. It stores primitives and attributes

Answer: B. A, C and D describe graphics.

17. A 16 × 16 monochrome bitmap needs
  • A. 16 bytes
  • B. 32 bytes
  • C. 256 bytes
  • D. 2,048 bytes

Answer: B. 256 pixels × 1 bit = 256 bits = 32 bytes.

18. How many colours does an 8-bit pixel allow?
  • A. 8
  • B. 128
  • C. 256
  • D. 65,536

Answer: C. 2⁸ = 256.

19. Which pair describes graphics formats?
  • A. Pixels and resolution
  • B. Primitives and attributes
  • C. Dpi and bit depth
  • D. Fields and frames

Answer: B. Graphics formats are specified through primitives (lines, circles, polyhedra) and attributes (line style, width, colour).

20. Which technique suits devices that cannot display individual dots, such as laser printers?
  • A. Dispersed-dot ordered dithering
  • B. Clustered-dot ordered dithering
  • C. Edge detection
  • D. Pulse code modulation

Answer: B. Dispersed-dot dithering is for devices (such as CRTs) that can display individual dots.

21. In image recognition, which step compares objects with stored models?
  • A. Conditioning
  • B. Labeling
  • C. Extracting
  • D. Matching

Answer: D. Matching compares each object with stored models and selects the best match.

22. Which statement about image transmission is correct?
  • A. It is dominated by time dependence, like video
  • B. It is bursty and needs reliable transport
  • C. It never uses compression
  • D. Its size is always equal to the structure size

Answer: B. A is false (time dependence is not dominant), C is false (JPEG/MPEG are used), and D is true only for symbolic transmission.

docs.title: Image Synthesis and Graphics Systems
docs.text: Unit 3Notes6 min read

docs.title: Computer image processing
docs.text:
Two linked ideas, opposite in direction:

  • Computer graphics is the pictorial synthesis of real or imaginary objects from their computer-based models.
  • Image processing is the converse: analysis of scenes, or reconstruction of models from pictures of 2D and 3D objects.

Computer image processing therefore has two parts: image synthesis (generation) and image analysis (recognition).

flowchart LR
    M["Model (data, primitives)"] -->|"Image synthesis (computer graphics)"| P["Picture"]
    P -->|"Image analysis (image processing)"| M2["Description / model"]

docs.title: Image synthesis
docs.text: Image synthesis deals with the generation of images of real or imaginary objects. It is an integral part of all computer user interfaces and is indispensable for visualising 2D, 3D and higher-dimensional objects.

docs.title: Applications of image synthesis
docs.text: Area Examples User interface Point-and-click facility; menu-driven systems; GUI windows with icons and menu items Office automation and electronic publishing Desktop publishing; electronic publishing; hypermedia systems Simulation and animation for scientific visualisation and entertainment Simulation of real-time systems; visualising the time-varying behaviour of systems; abstract representation of complex mathematical expressions; models for fluid flow and chemical reaction; cartoons; flying logos and exciting visuals for movies

docs.title: Dynamics in graphics
docs.text:
Graphics are not limited to static images; they can vary dynamically. A user can control an animation by adjusting its speed or changing the visible part of a scene. Dynamics are therefore an integral part of (dynamic) graphics. Two kinds:

Motion dynamics Update dynamics Meaning Objects are moved or activated relative to a static observer's viewpoint. Objects may also be static while their environment moves. The actual change of shape, colour or other properties of the objects being viewed Example Flight simulator Deformation of an in-flight aeroplane structure

Interactive versus non-interactive graphics : non-interactive graphics is passive, with no communication between user and computer (the user has no control; a screen saver is the example). Interactive graphics involves communication between user and computer.

docs.title: Framework of an interactive graphics system
docs.text:
The high-level framework of almost any interactive graphics system (for example SRGP) has three software components. Some sources add a fourth part, the graphics hardware.

flowchart LR
    AM["Application model (application database)"] --> AP["Application program"]
    AP -->|"Graphics output commands"| GS["Graphics system"]
    GS --> HW["Graphics hardware (display)"]
    HW -.->|"User input"| GS
    GS -.->|"Input transformations"| AP

docs.title: 1. Application model
docs.text:
• Represents the data or objects to be pictured on the screen.
  • Typically stores descriptions of primitives that define the shape of components, the object attributes, and connectivity relationships describing how the components fit together.
  • Stored in an application database.
  • It is application-specific and created independently of any display system.

docs.title: 2. Application program
docs.text:
Converts the primitive descriptions in the application model into the procedure calls or commands the graphics system uses to create an image. This takes two steps:

  1. Extraction of the portions to be viewed from the application database, using a selection or query system.
  2. Conversion of the extracted geometry into the proper format.

The program produces views by sending the graphics system a series of graphics output commands.

docs.title: 3. Graphics system
docs.text:
The intermediary between the application program and the display hardware, responsible for actually producing the picture. It performs two kinds of transformation:

  • Output transformations: from objects in the application model to a view of the model.
  • Input transformations: from user actions to application-program inputs that cause the model and/or picture to change.

Exam tip

"Explain the framework of an interactive graphics system" is a standard question. Name the three components and give one line of purpose for each, including the two steps of the application program and the two transformations of the graphics system.

docs.title: Input devices
docs.text:
• 2D input: mouse, keyboard, data tablet, touch-sensitive panel on the screen.
  • 3D and higher-dimensional input: trackballs, spaceballs, data glove.
  • Even audio communication can provide input.

docs.title: Output: the raster display
docs.text:
Modern visual output uses raster display devices, which display primitives in special buffers called refresh buffers as pixel components.

  • A raster display uses a CRT with rows of phosphor dots; electron guns at the back make the dots glow when hit.
  • The complete display is a raster of horizontal raster lines, each made of pixels.
  • The electron beam moves across the screen one row at a time, top to bottom. The picture information is held in the refresh buffer.
  • The video controller reads the refresh buffer and produces the image, turning the phosphor spots on and off according to the image data. It samples the entire screen line by line.
  • After each row the beam returns to the start of the next row: this is the horizontal retrace.
  • A display controller receives and interprets the sequence of output commands. In low-end systems such as personal computers it is implemented in software, as part of a graphics library, and the refresh buffer is part of CPU memory.

A typical diagram shows the computer host interface sending display commands to the display controller, which writes the scanned image into the refresh buffer; the video controller reads that buffer and drives the monitor; mouse and keyboard send interaction data back to the display controller.

flowchart LR
    H["Computer host interface"] -->|"Display commands"| DC["Display controller"]
    DC <--> RB["Refresh buffer (scanned image)"]
    RB --> VC["Video controller"]
    VC --> MON["Monitor"]
    KM["Keyboard, mouse"] -->|"Interaction data"| DC

docs.title: Dithering
docs.text:
Dithering is a process used in output devices (monitor screens and some printers) to produce shades of gray or tints of colour. The aim is an effect as close to the original image as possible while using fewer colours.

It relies on the eye's spatial integration: if we view a very small area from a large enough distance, the eye averages the fine detail and records only the overall intensity.

Dithering is usually called halftoning, and the shades of gray are called halftones.

docs.title: Dither matrix
docs.text:
If a pixel is replaced by an m × n dither matrix (an array of dots), the pixel can show intensity levels from 0 to m × n (that is, the number of dots lit).

A 2 × 2 matrix can represent 5 intensity levels: none, one, two, three or all four dots lit.

docs.title: Two techniques
docs.text: Clustered-dot ordered dithering (halftoning) Dispersed-dot ordered dithering How it works Four adjacent pixels represent the intensity of a single colour; lighting none, one, two, three or all four gives different intensities Uses a 2 × 2 dither pattern with halftone patterns as in the clustered method Used for Devices that cannot display individual dots, e.g. laser printers Devices that can display individual dots, e.g. CRT displays Result Different intensities of a colour A colour CRT shows 125 colours

docs.title: The 125-colour calculation
docs.text:
Each of the three channels (red, green, blue) can show 5 intensities with a 2 × 2 pattern, so:

\[5 \times 5 \times 5 = 125 \text{ colour combinations}\]

A contradictory phrase

One source says dithering is "done by random arrangement of pixels". The main notes describe ordered dithering (clustered-dot and dispersed-dot). Use ordered in the exam.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
Differentiate motion dynamics and update dynamics.

Motion dynamics: objects move or are activated relative to a static observer (flight simulator). Update dynamics: the shape, colour or other properties of the objects change (deformation of an aeroplane structure in flight).

Name the three software components of an interactive graphics system.

The application model, the application program and the graphics system.

How can a 2 × 2 dither pattern give 125 colours?

A 2 × 2 pattern gives 5 intensities per channel (0 to 4 dots lit). With red, green and blue channels: 5 × 5 × 5 = 125 colours.

docs.title: Unit 4: Video and Animation
docs.text:
4 hours · approx. weeks 4–5

Ready

Topic notes, practice questions and class slides are complete for this unit.

docs.title: What this unit covers
docs.text:
Syllabus topic Notes page 4.1 Basic video concepts: video signal representation Video and Visual Representation 4.1 Transmission (RGB, YUV, YIQ, composite) and digitization Video Transmission and Digitization 4.1 Computer video format Computer Video Format 4.2 Basic animation concepts Animation Basics 4.2 Animation languages and control Animation Languages and Control 4.2 Display and transmission of animation Animation Display and Transmission

Also: Class Slides and Practice Questions.

docs.title: Formulas to memorise
docs.text:
Quantity Formula Effective vertical resolution active scan lines × Kell factor (0.7) Required horizontal resolution aspect ratio × effective vertical resolution Video bandwidth a × b × c / 2 Luminance Y = 0.30R + 0.59G + 0.11B Raw frame size width × height × bits per pixel Raw data rate frame size × frame rate

Where marks come from

Expect one numerical question (raw video size, bandwidth or Kell factor), one on RGB/YUV/YIQ/composite, one on flicker and continuity of motion, and one on animation control or display (double buffering, symbolic vs pixmap).

Before the next class

Read Video and Visual Representation and be ready to explain why 25 or 30 fps is needed and why 50 Hz is the flicker limit.

docs.title: Animation Basics
docs.text: Unit 4Notes2 min read

docs.title: What is animation?
docs.text:
• Animation is making something look and feel alive: it covers all changes that have a visual effect (time-varying position, shape, colour, transparency, structure, texture).
  • Computer-based animation is done with a computer having graphical tools; similar images are displayed quickly. It is based on the keyframe concept: a keyframe holds the positions (begin and end of a transition) of the objects.

Two categories:

Motion dynamics Update dynamics Induces life by Changing the position of an object Changing the shape, size or structure Example Bouncing ball Flower blooming from a bud

docs.title: Stages of the process
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    I["Input process: digitize drawings"] --> C["Composition: combine foreground, background, effects"]
    C --> P["Pencil test"]
    P --> B["In-betweening"]
    B --> L["Changing colours (CLUT)"]
  1. Input process: drawings must be digitized (optical scanning, data tablet or drawing program) and filtered to clean up glitches.
  2. Composition stage: separate elements (foreground characters, background scenery, special effects) are combined into the final frames.
  3. Pencil test: checks the animation is correct, using an animation camera, before cleaning and painting the drawings. Pan and zoom effects slowly zoom in on a subject and pan between subjects.
  4. In-between process: frames with intermediate positions between key frames are composed.
  5. Changing colours: using the CLUT.

docs.title: In-betweening and interpolation
docs.text:
• Computer in-betweening uses interpolation (lerping, linear interpolation): given start and end positions, intermediate positions are computed on a straight line.
  • Lerp is the easiest method but gives unrealistic motion. Example: a ball thrown in the air with only three key frames would move in straight segments instead of an arc.
  • Splines are used to smooth the interpolation between key frames.
\[P(t) = (1-t)\,P_{start} + t\,P_{end}, \quad 0 \le t \le 1\]

Extra

The lerp formula is standard. Example: start x = 0, end x = 100, 5 in-betweens means t = 1/6, 2/6, …: x ≈ 16.7, 33.3, 50, 66.7, 83.3.

docs.title: Changing colours with a CLUT
docs.text:
• Colours are changed by manipulating the colour look-up table in the frame buffer. The simplest method is to cycle the colours in the table, changing the colour of various parts of the image.
  • CLUT animation is faster than sending a whole new pixmap to the frame buffer for every frame.

Watch out

Do not mix up the input process (digitizing drawings) with in-betweening (computing intermediate frames).

Exam tip

Typical questions: "What is in-betweening? Why are splines used?" and "Explain CLUT animation." Give the lerp weakness (ball path) explicitly.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
Differentiate motion dynamics and update dynamics.

Motion dynamics changes position (bouncing ball); update dynamics changes shape, size or structure (flower blooming).

Why is lerp not enough for a thrown ball?

It joins key positions by straight lines, so the path is unrealistic; splines give a smooth curve.

Why is CLUT animation fast?

Only the small table is changed instead of sending a new pixmap for each frame.

docs.title: Animation Display and Transmission
docs.text: Unit 4Notes2 min read

docs.title: Display of animation
docs.text:
• Animated objects (lines, polygons, …) must be scan-converted into a pixmap in the frame buffer. To show a rotating object, successive views from slightly different positions are scan-converted one after another.
  • A raster screen sweeps one row at a time, top to bottom; the refresh buffer holds the intensity values for the next picture.
  • Scan conversion must be done at least 10 (preferably 15 to 20) times per second, so a new image must be created in no more than 100 ms.
  • Erasing and redrawing within that time is impossible with a single buffer; it gives a distracting effect.

docs.title: Double buffering
docs.text:
• Solution: two buffers (the two halves of the pixmap: image0 and image1). One is displayed while the next frame is built in the other; then they swap.
  • Increases throughput and gives more realistic animation.
flowchart LR
    A["Frame n displayed from image0"] --> B["Meanwhile frame n+1 drawn into image1"]
    B --> C["Swap roles"]
    C --> A

docs.title: Transmission of animation
docs.text:
Two approaches:

Symbolic representation Pixmap representation What is sent Objects (e.g. circle for a ball) plus operations (roll the ball), as text Scan-converted images of the objects Transmission time Short (small size) Longer Display time Longer (receiver must generate the pixmaps) Shorter Rate depends on Size of the object structure + size of the operation-command structure + number of objects and commands per second Size of one pixmap × images per second
  • A pixmap is a rectangular array of pixel colour values; with 1 bit per pixel it is a bitmap.

Pixmap rate

320 × 240, 8 bits, 15 images/s: 76,800 bytes × 15 = 1,152,000 bytes/s ≈ 1.1 MB/s.

Exam tip

The standard 5-mark question compares symbolic and pixmap transmission on transmission time vs display time.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
Why is double buffering needed?

A single buffer cannot erase, redraw and show a frame within 100 ms (or 50 ms), causing distracting effects; two buffers allow one to display while the other is filled.

Which transmission method has faster display?

Pixmap: it is directly displayed, but takes longer to transmit.

docs.title: Animation Languages and Control
docs.text: Unit 4Notes3 min read

docs.title: 1. Linear-list notations
docs.text:
Text-based scripts where each event gives start frame, end frame and action, written sequentially like a list. Easy to follow; used in early multimedia and timeline-based engines.

Example

42, 53, B, ROTATE "PALM", 1, 30 means: between frames 42 and 53 rotate the object PALM about axis 1 by 30 degrees, the amount per frame being taken from table B.

Examples: Scefo (SCEne FOrmat); SMIL (Synchronized Multimedia Integration Language) with <seq> and <par>; a traffic light script: 00s setColor light RED, 05s … YELLOW, 07s … GREEN, 12s … RED.

docs.title: 2. General-purpose languages
docs.text: Animation capability embedded in a general programming language; variables of the language serve as parameters of animation routines. Example: ASAS, built on LISP, with many geometric transformations.

docs.title: 3. Graphical languages
docs.text:
Textual languages cannot visualise action. Graphical languages let the animator provide a picture of the action, to express, edit and understand simultaneous changes. Examples: GENESYS, DIAL, S-Dynamics System.

Category Describes by Example Linear list Event list with frame numbers Scefo, SMIL General purpose Program code ASAS Graphical Pictures of actions GENESYS, DIAL, S-Dynamics

docs.title: Methods of controlling animation
docs.text:
Control is independent of the language used to describe the animation.

Method Idea Example Full explicit control Simplest. Animator describes everything (scaling, translation, rotation or key frames plus interpolation), possibly by mouse, joystick, data glove BBOP (3D key-frame figure animation) Procedural control Objects communicate to determine properties; position of one object affects another Balls cannot pass through walls; actors pass positions to other actors Constraint-based Animator sets constraints; system solves for motion obeying all. Compound, non-linear motion of objects in contact Sutherland's Sketchpad; character rigging, robotics Tracking live action Trajectories taken from real motion Rotoscoping; markers on a body; data glove Kinematics and dynamics Describe motion by position/velocity (kinematics) or by forces (dynamics) Cube example below

docs.title: Tracking live action
docs.text:
• Rotoscoping: film of people or animals acting the parts; animators draw over the film, replacing the actors with animated equivalents.
  • Indicators on key body points: tracked positions give locations for the matching points of an animated model. A data glove measures hand position and orientation and the flexion and hyperextension of each finger.

docs.title: Kinematics vs dynamics
docs.text:
• Kinematics: position and velocity of points. "The cube is at the origin at t = 0 and moves with constant acceleration in direction (1, 1, 5)."
  • Dynamics: includes the physical laws (Newton): acceleration is proportional to force, the constant being the mass. "At t = 0 the cube is at (0, 100, 0) m, has mass 100 g, and gravity acts on it."
  • Knowing kinematics and dynamics at a point lets us determine the next point of the motion.

Exam tip

"Explain any three methods of controlling animation" is common: pick explicit, procedural and constraint-based, with one example each.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
Give one example each of a linear-list, general-purpose and graphical language.

Scefo (or SMIL); ASAS; GENESYS (or S-Dynamics).

What is rotoscoping?

Drawing over film of live actors so that the animated characters copy their motion.

Differentiate kinematics and dynamics.

Kinematics: position and velocity. Dynamics: adds the physical laws and forces (mass, gravity).

docs.title: Computer Video Format
docs.text: Unit 4Notes2 min read

docs.title: Standard for digitization: CCIR-601
docs.text:
The ITU-R (International Telecommunications Union – Radiocommunications Branch) defined Recommendation CCIR-601 to standardise digitization of video pictures. Variants exist for TV broadcasting, video telephony and videoconferencing.

Video digitizers differ in image resolution, quantization and frame rate. Example: SGI VINO digitizer for NTSC: 640 × 480, 8 bits/pixel, 4 frames/second.

docs.title: Raster display architecture
docs.text:
The output of digitized video depends on the input and output devices; the most common display is the raster display.

flowchart LR
    G["Graphics program"] --> D["Display controller"]
    D --> R["Refresh buffer (frame buffer)"]
    R --> V["Video controller"]
    V --> M["Monitor"]
  • The graphics program creates the high-level image interactively. The display controller interprets display commands and writes pixel values into the refresh buffer.
  • The video controller is hardware that reads the pixel values in time-synchronism with the scanning and converts them into red, green and blue analog signals for the display. It can also access memory.

docs.title: Colour look-up table (CLUT)
docs.text: A range of colour values is stored in a table; each pixel value is an address into the table, which holds the corresponding three colour values. This is the colour look-up table. It saves frame-buffer memory and allows colour changes by editing the table (see Animation Basics).

docs.title: Video controller standards
docs.text:
CGA (Color Graphics Adapter) · EGA (Enhanced Graphics Adapter) · VGA (Video Graphics Array) · 8514/A display adapter mode · XGA (Extended Graphics Array) · Super VGA (SVGA).

Extra

The resolution table of these standards is often shown only as a picture. Commonly quoted: CGA 320 × 200 (4 colours), EGA 640 × 350 (16), VGA 640 × 480 (16) or 320 × 200 (256), SVGA 800 × 600 and above. Check against your textbook before quoting.

docs.title: Video file formats
docs.text:
Video formats use lossy compression to cut file size while keeping quality.

Format Extension Codec support Common use MP4 .mp4 H.264, H.265 Streaming, mobile devices MOV .mov H.264 Apple ecosystem, editing AVI .avi Various Legacy PC playback MKV .mkv Any Flexible storage WebM .webm VP9, AV1 Web streaming (royalty-free)

docs.title: Raw video size
docs.text:
\[\text{Frame size} = \text{width} \times \text{height} \times \text{bits per pixel}$$ $$\text{Data rate} = \text{frame size} \times \text{frame rate}\]

Worked example: PAL, 352 × 288, 16 bits/pixel, 25 fps

  • Frame size = 352 × 288 × 16 = 1,622,016 bits (= 202,752 bytes, about 202.5 KB with decimal kilobytes).
  • Data rate = 1,622,016 × 25 = 40,550,400 bits/s.
  • In MB/s: 40,550,400 ÷ (8 × 1024 × 1024) = 4.83 MB/s.

Units

Be consistent: state whether you use 1000 or 1024 for KB and MB. For example 202,752 bytes ÷ 1024 = 198 KB.

Quick practice

640 × 480, 24-bit, 30 fps: frame = 921,600 bytes; rate = 27,648,000 bytes/s ≈ 26.4 MB/s; one minute ≈ 1.55 GB.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
What does the video controller do?

Reads pixel values from the refresh buffer in step with the scan and converts them into R, G, B analog signals for the monitor.

What is a CLUT?

A table whose entries hold colour values; the pixel value is the address into the table.

docs.title: Unit 4: Practice Questions
docs.text:
Unit 4Practice5 min read

Write your own answer on paper first, then click to reveal the model answer. Marks are a guide to how much detail the question deserves.

docs.title: Short answer
docs.text:
1. Define video and frame rate. (3 marks)

Video is a combination of image and audio: a sequence of still frames shown at a fixed speed, the frame rate in fps. Because of persistence of vision the frames merge into apparent motion; 20 to 30 fps looks smooth.

2. State the three aspects of video signal representation. (3 marks)

Visual representation, transmission and digitization.

3. What is the Kell factor? Compute the effective vertical resolution for 576 active lines. (4 marks)

Some detail falls between scan lines, so only about 70 % of the vertical resolution is usable: the Kell factor 0.7. 576 × 0.7 = 403.2 lines. Required horizontal resolution for 4:3 = 4/3 × 403.2 = 537.6.

4. Define aspect ratio. Why must it be preserved? (2 marks)

Picture width ÷ height (4/3 for TV, 16/9 widescreen). If it differs between source and display the picture looks too wide or too narrow.

5. What is flicker and how is it avoided? (4 marks)

Periodic brightness fluctuation when the refresh rate is too low. Minimum refresh to avoid it: 50 Hz. Avoid by raising the refresh rate or by interlaced scanning (odd lines then even lines, two fields per frame).

6. Calculate the video bandwidth for a = 1312, b = 800, c = 100 Hz. (3 marks)

a × b × c / 2 = 1312 × 800 × 100 / 2 = 52.48 MHz. The division by 2 is because two adjacent pixels are scanned per cycle.

7. Calculate the raw frame size and data rate for 352 × 288, 16 bits/pixel, 25 fps. (4 marks)

Frame = 352 × 288 × 16 = 1,622,016 bits (202,752 bytes). Rate = × 25 = 40,550,400 bits/s ≈ 4.83 MB/s (÷ 8 × 1024 × 1024).

8. Differentiate component and composite video signals. (4 marks)

Component (RGB, YUV, YIQ): separate signals, best quality, more bandwidth/wires. Composite: luminance and chrominance mixed into one carrier, cheaper, but interference between them, reduced by modulation.

9. Why is YUV used instead of RGB for broadcast? (3 marks)

Eye is more sensitive to luminance than chrominance; U and V can be scaled down to save bandwidth, and Y alone gives a black-and-white picture for old sets.

10. Write the equations for Y, U and V. (2 marks)

Y = 0.30R + 0.59G + 0.11B; U = 0.493(B − Y); V = 0.877(R − Y).

11. Define sampling and quantizing. (2 marks)

Sampling digitizes the spatial position (M × N points); quantizing digitizes the colour/brightness values.

12. Differentiate motion dynamics and update dynamics. (3 marks)

Motion dynamics: change of position (bouncing ball). Update dynamics: change of shape, size or structure (flower blooming).

13. What is in-betweening? Why are splines preferred to lerp? (4 marks)

Creating frames with intermediate positions between key frames. Lerp joins key positions by straight lines (a thrown ball with three keys moves unrealistically). Splines smooth the interpolation.

14. What is a pencil test? (2 marks)

A check that the animation is correct, done with an animation camera before cleaning and painting the drawings; pan and zoom can be applied.

15. Explain CLUT animation. (3 marks)

Colours are changed by cycling or editing the entries of the colour look-up table in the frame buffer, recolouring parts of the image; faster than sending a new pixmap each frame.

docs.title: Long answer
docs.text:
16. Explain the nine measures of visual representation of video. (8 marks)

Vertical detail and viewing distance (scan lines, Kell factor 0.7); horizontal detail and picture width (bandwidth, aspect ratio); total detail (vertical × horizontal elements); depth perception (perspective, focal length); luminance and chrominance (Y, U, V); temporal aspects of illumination; continuity of motion (>15 fps, 30 fps for filmed, 24 fps film, NTSC 29.97, PAL 25); flicker (≥ 50 Hz, interlacing); temporal aspect of bandwidth (a·b·c/2, 1/25 s per frame).

17. Explain RGB, YUV, YIQ and composite signals. (8 marks)

Describe each as in Video Transmission: RGB for monitors, best colour but more bandwidth; YUV with equations and scaled chrominance; YIQ for NTSC with Q needing less bandwidth; composite all in one carrier with interference and modulation.

18. Explain the raster display architecture and the role of the video controller and CLUT. (6 marks)

Graphics program → display controller (writes pixels into refresh buffer) → video controller (reads buffer in sync with scan, uses CLUT to turn pixel values into R, G, B analog signals) → monitor. CLUT: pixel value as an address to three colour values.

19. Explain the three categories of animation languages with examples. (6 marks)

Linear list (frame numbers + event, Scefo/SMIL, the PALM example), general purpose (embedded in a programming language, ASAS on LISP), graphical (picture of action, GENESYS, DIAL, S-Dynamics).

20. Describe any four methods of controlling animation. (8 marks)

Full explicit control (BBOP), procedural control, constraint-based (Sketchpad), tracking live action (rotoscoping, data glove), kinematics and dynamics. One paragraph each.

21. Explain display of animation and double buffering. (6 marks)

Objects scan-converted into pixmap; at least 10 (preferably 15–20) per second so ≤ 100 ms per image; single buffer cannot erase/redraw in time; use two buffers, display one while building the other.

22. Compare symbolic and pixmap transmission of animation. (6 marks)

Use the table in Display and Transmission.
