docs.title: System Software
docs.text:
Unit 11Notes2 min read

Instead of a separate library per device, device access becomes part of the operating system. Continuous-data processing needs real-time schedulers (see Unit 7).

docs.title: Example: the Nemo system
docs.text:
Nemo consists of the Nemo Trusted Supervisor Call (NTSC) running in supervisor mode and three domains in user mode: system, device drivers and application.

Not the TV standard

NTSC here means Nemo Trusted Supervisor Call. It has nothing to do with the NTSC television standard of Unit 4.

  • The NTSC code implements the functions needed by user-mode processes and supports three kinds of processes:
    • System processes: implement most of the OS services.
    • Device processes: like system processes but attached to device interrupt stubs that run in supervisor mode.
    • Application processes: contain user programs.
  • NTSC calls are in two classes: calls only a privileged system process (for example the kernel) may execute, and calls any process may execute.
  • NTSC provides the interface between a multimedia hardware device and its driver process, so even a device with only a low-level hardware interface can be used.
  • Processes talk through IPC (inter-process communication), built on low-level events and, if needed, shared memory.

docs.title: Data as time capsules
docs.text: A time capsule is an abstraction related to file systems: a file extension for storing, modifying and accessing continuous media. Each LDU carries, besides its data type and value, its valid life span. The concept is used more for video than for audio.

docs.title: Data as streams
docs.text:
A stream is the continuous flow of audio and video data. It is established between a source and a sink before the flow starts. Operations on a stream: play, fast forward, rewind, stop.

In Microsoft Windows the Media Control Interface (MCI) gives access to continuous media streams and their devices.

Exam tip

Define time capsule (data plus life span), stream (source to sink), and name MCI. If Nemo is asked, give supervisor call plus three domains and three process types.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
What does a time capsule contain?

Each LDU's data type, value and valid life span.

What is MCI?

The Media Control Interface of Microsoft Windows for accessing continuous media streams and devices.

docs.title: Toolkits and Higher Programming Languages
docs.text: Unit 11Notes2 min read

docs.title: Toolkits
docs.text:
Toolkits control audio and video processing in a programming environment. They represent interfaces at the system-software level, can be embedded into programming languages or object-oriented environments, and are used to:

  • abstract from the physical layer;
  • give a uniform interface for all different continuous-media devices;
  • introduce the client-server paradigm;
  • hide process structures.

It would be valuable to have the same toolkit on all platforms, but experience shows this remains a wish and would reduce performance.

docs.title: Higher programming languages
docs.text:
In a higher (high-level) language (HLL), processing of continuous media is done by groups of similarly built functions. The calls are mostly hardware and driver independent. Programs either access multimedia data structures directly or communicate with the active processes of the real-time environment; devices are controlled through drivers.

Media can be seen in three ways inside a language.

docs.title: 1. Media as types
docs.text:
Audio and video are data types, just as character is the type for text (the smallest addressable element). A program can copy, compare, delete, read, store and display them, and use them in other data structures. Example (OCCAM-2, derived from Communicating Sequential Processes for transputers): two audio LDUs from two microphones are read in parallel and mixed:

a, b REAL;
ldu.left1, ldu.left2, ldu.left_mixed AUDIO_LDU;
WHILE
  COBEGIN
    PROCESS_1  Input(micro1, ldu.left1)
    PROCESS_2  Input(micro2, ldu.left2)
  ldu.left_mixed := a * ldu.left1 + b * ldu.left2;
END WHILE

docs.title: 2. Media as files
docs.text:
A continuous stream is treated as a file: open associates a device with a file name and returns a file descriptor; read, mix, activate, deactivate and close follow.

file_h1 = open(MICROPHONE_1, ...)
file_h2 = open(MICROPHONE_2, ...)
file_h3 = open(SPEAKER, ...)
read(file_h1); read(file_h2)
mix(file_h3, file_h1, file_h2)
activate(file_h1, file_h2, file_h3)
...
deactivate(...);  rc1 = close(file_h1) ...

Difference from discrete files: continuous read/write keep assigning new values continuously to a variable bound to one read, whereas for discrete data each read call fetches the next value.

docs.title: 3. Media as processes
docs.text:
Processing continuous data is time dependent: the life span of a process equals the life span of a connection between source and destination (local or remote). The process is created, reserves the devices at creation, and its actions are controlled by IPC messages:

PROCESS cont_process_a;
  on_message_do
    set_volume ...
    set_loudness ...
pid = create(cont_process_a)
send(pid, set_volume, 3)
send(pid, set_loudness)

docs.title: Language requirements
docs.text:
• The HLL must support parallel processing; the number of processes is known at compile time, and processes can also be defined dynamically at run time.
  • The IPC mechanism must transmit audio and video in time (they have a limited life span). It must:
    • understand a priori or implicitly specified time requirements;
    • transmit the data according to those requirements;
    • start processing the received data on time.
  • Language: the authors see no demand for a new dedicated language. Replacing a language is difficult because cooperation between the real-time environment and other programs needs semantic changes. A language extension is proposed, a simple language meeting the requirements; examples: OCCAM-2, Ada, parallel C variants for transputers.
View Media is a Typical operations Types Data type (like char) Assign, copy, mix with operators Files File open, read, write, activate, close Processes Process (life span = connection) create, send messages

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
Name the three views of media in a programming language.

As types, as files, as processes.

What must the IPC mechanism of a real-time language do?

Understand time requirements, transmit continuous data according to them, and start processing on time.

docs.title: Application Areas in Detail
docs.text:
Unit 12Notes3 min read

Extra

The course material covers application classes, system types and components and the development cycle only. This page is written from standard textbook knowledge to cover the rest of syllabus 12.1–12.4. Check details against your prescribed textbook.

docs.title: 12.1 Video on demand (VoD)
docs.text:
Video on demand lets a user select and watch a video at any time, with VCR-like controls (play, pause, fast forward, rewind).

flowchart LR
    S["Video server (disk arrays, archive)"] --> N["Network (cable, ADSL, fibre, Internet)"] --> B["Set-top box / PC"] --> TV["TV / display"]
Type Meaning True VoD Each user gets an individual stream, started instantly, full interactivity Near VoD The same film is started on several channels at staggered times (for example every 15 min); users wait for the next start; much cheaper

Requirements: large server storage and bandwidth (MPEG-1 about 1.5 Mbit/s, MPEG-2 about 4 to 6 Mbit/s per stream), real-time disk scheduling, admission control and QoS guarantees, billing and security.

Server capacity

A server with 1 Gbit/s output can serve about 1,000 ÷ 4 = 250 MPEG-2 streams at 4 Mbit/s each.

docs.title: 12.2 Video conferencing
docs.text:
Video conferencing carries audio and video (plus shared tools) between two or more sites in real time.

  • Point to point and multipoint (a multipoint control unit, MCU, mixes or switches streams).
  • Desktop and room-based systems; features: shared whiteboard, application sharing, file transfer, chat.
  • Requirements: low delay (about 150 ms or less), small jitter, lip synchronisation (±80 ms), bandwidth adaptation, echo cancellation.
  • Standards: H.320 (ISDN), H.323 (packet networks), H.261 video coding (Unit 5), and SIP with RTP today.

docs.title: 12.3 Educational and industrial applications
docs.text:
Educational: computer-based training (CBT), e-learning and virtual classrooms, simulations and virtual laboratories, educational games, multimedia encyclopedias, interactive tutorials with self-assessment. Benefits: self-paced, rich explanation with animation and video, immediate feedback. Limits: development cost and the need for good instructional design.

Industrial: employee training and safety simulations, product demonstration and catalogues, kiosks, CAD/CAM visualisation, process monitoring with video and sensor data, remote maintenance with video and annotation, corporate presentations.

docs.title: 12.4 Information systems, archives, entertainment, editors, trends
docs.text:
Information systems (kiosks): public touch-screen terminals giving maps, timetables, tourist and government information; need simple navigation and robust hardware.

Multimedia archives and digital libraries: collections of text, images, audio and video stored digitally with metadata. Needs: digitisation and compression, indexing (text, content-based retrieval of images and video), search, long-term preservation, access control and copyright, distributed access over networks. Examples: national archives, museum collections, film and music archives.

Media entertainment: computer games, interactive and digital TV, music and video streaming, special effects in films, theme-park rides.

Media editors: tools to create and modify media: image editors (Photoshop), audio editors, non-linear video editors (cut, effects, transitions on a timeline), animation tools (Flash, Maya), authoring tools that integrate media.

Trends: streaming and mobile multimedia, high-definition and 4K video with efficient codecs, virtual, augmented and mixed reality, cloud-based services, AI-assisted creation, search and captioning, 5G low-latency networks, social and user-generated media.

Exam tip

For "short notes", give a definition, a block diagram or a list of requirements, and two examples. For VoD always name true vs near VoD.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
Differentiate true and near video on demand.

True: separate stream per user, immediate start. Near: staggered start times on shared channels.

List the requirements of a digital library.

Digitisation and compression, indexing and retrieval, preservation, access control and copyright, networked access.

docs.title: Application Classes
docs.text:
Unit 12Notes2 min read

Class Description Game systems The leaders in using multimedia technology because the market is very large and demands on quality, although intense, are not crucial to the success Multimedia repositories Mostly play-back-only systems. End users do not usually add information; input and output of the workflow are independent. Like games, but the database is much larger and the data needs indexing Interactive TV and video on demand Usually developed from cable TV technology. The set-top box connects the digital network to the TV and other home appliances (telephone, fax). Besides the cable converter function it offers a full interactive multimedia interface to services; standardising the interfaces (set-top box to network and to home appliance) is critical Video/phone conferencing and hypermedia mail Seeing the other person is a major improvement over voice only. More functions: interactive whiteboard, sharing paper-based diagrams, sharing computer output. Video messages are kept longer than voice messages, so need much more storage Shared workspaces and executive environments Shared workspace: a user runs applications and the output appears on screens at remote locations. Shared executive environment: users at different places run the same application on their own workstation with the same data Business process workflow applications Depend on the business process being served. Traditional relational databases must be extended to handle multimedia elements; object-oriented databases are a more natural medium for multimedia objects 
flowchart TB
    A["Multimedia applications"] --> G["Game systems"]
    A --> R["Repositories"]
    A --> I["Interactive TV / VoD"]
    A --> V["Video and phone conferencing, hypermedia mail"]
    A --> S["Shared workspace, executive environment"]
    A --> B["Business workflow"]

Exam tip

Learn one distinguishing sentence per class: games = big market; repositories = play-back only, indexed; interactive TV = set-top box; conferencing = whiteboard, sharing; shared workspace vs shared executive environment; workflow = object-oriented databases.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
Differentiate shared workspace and shared executive environment.

Shared workspace: one site runs the application, others see its output. Shared executive environment: each site runs the same application locally on the same data.

What is a set-top box?

The device connecting the digital network to the TV and home appliances, providing interactive multimedia services.

docs.title: The Multimedia Development Cycle
docs.text:
Unit 12Notes4 min read

flowchart LR
    P["1. Planning and costing"] --> D["2. Designing"] --> V["3. Developing and producing"] --> T["4. Testing and debugging"] --> L["5. Delivering"]

docs.title: 1. Planning and costing
docs.text:
Main concerns:

  • capture the ideas and requirements of you or your clients;
  • identify the potential audience and users;
  • find the benefit of developing the application;
  • evaluate feasibility and cost of the whole project (production, testing, delivery).

A "back-of-the-envelope" or "paper napkin" approach is often used: capture ideas and judge feasibility quickly. The most important considerations:

Factor Points Hardware The most common limiting factor for development time and end users: poor or no sound device, limited storage, very narrow network bandwidth Software Development software is expensive; software needed by end users adds up Contents Existing material may not match needs, may be copyrighted (permission may be refused); new material is expensive and slow Skills Very broad: computer, artistic and application-domain skills

It helps to build a pilot project or prototype first.

docs.title: 2. Designing
docs.text: A creative activity needing computer skills, talent in graphic arts, video and music, and knowledge of the subject area.

docs.title: Storyboarding
docs.text: A storyboard describes the project in exact detail with words and sketches for each screen image, sound and navigational choice. It can be very detailed (every screen down to colour, shade, text and attributes) or only a schematic guide, drawn on paper or with a computer tool.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
The arrangement of the multimedia information; a well-organised document lets users find information efficiently; start early. Types:

Architecture Structure Linear One path from start to end Hierarchical Tree of menus and sub-menus Non-linear Free links between nodes (hypermedia) Composite A mix of the above

docs.title: User interface
docs.text:
The emphasis is on multimedia presentation; content selection is the key and is limited by the size and complexity of the presentation, the quality of information, display hardware limits, and the need for completeness and coherence. Media must be "adequate": to teach tennis, graphics and video suit better than text. Coordination means composing the media.

Interface techniques (the remote camera surveillance example: a camera server on a serial interface, a remote client sends commands, video is digitised, compressed and sent):

  • Keyboard: fixed commands on keys.
  • Buttons in a GUI: clicking "left" pans left.
  • Scroll bars beside the video window.
  • Special device: a joystick is more natural.
  • Direct manipulation of the video window: click a point to centre the camera there.

User-friendliness is the primary goal, though what it means and how to measure it are not always clear:

  • Easy to learn and easy to remember instructions (for occasional and daily users);
  • Effective instructions: logically connected functions presented together and similarly; graphical symbols beat text; media exchangeable between applications;
  • Prompt feedback after each user action;
  • Usable by professional and occasional users.

docs.title: 3. Developing and producing
docs.text: Production is when the project is actually rendered. Tasks: acquire all media elements, compose them according to the storyboard, track media elements and track progress, and have a way (or an expert) to solve technical problems quickly.

docs.title: Rights and permissions
docs.text: You must know who owns acquired content. There are nine types of protected works: literary, dramatic, musical, artistic works; sound recordings, cinematograph films, television broadcasts, sound broadcasts, published editions of works. License the rights before use; you may negotiate outright ownership or a licence. Questions to settle: how the material will be used and distributed; fixed period?; exclusive or non-exclusive?; where distributed?; does the owner have authority to assign rights?; remuneration?

docs.title: 4. Testing and debugging
docs.text:
An important and time-consuming phase.

Alpha testing Beta testing Who Internal, the in-house team A wider range of testers, representative of real users, not those who built it

The product is used by many users who know little about computers and on many platforms and configurations, so test widely.

docs.title: 5. Delivering
docs.text:
Plan delivery early. CD-ROM and the Internet are the two most popular means (today also app stores and streaming). Plan installation and use. The distribution must include all media elements (clips), runtime libraries (Director runtime), drivers (DirectX), helper programs (QuickTime viewer, Acrobat reader) and the installation program and compression/decompression programs.

Exam tip

The five stages are a certain question. Add storyboard, architectures and alpha/beta testing for full marks.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
Differentiate alpha and beta testing.

Alpha: internal, in-house testers. Beta: wider group of representative users who were not part of the production.

Name the four types of architecture.

Linear, hierarchical, non-linear, composite.

docs.title: Unit 12: Practice Questions
docs.text:
Unit 12Practice3 min read

Write your own answer on paper first, then click to reveal the model answer. Questions marked (textbook) depend on the page written from textbook knowledge.

docs.title: Short answer
docs.text:
1. List the classes of multimedia applications. (4 marks)

Game systems, multimedia repositories, interactive TV and video on demand, video/phone conferencing and hypermedia mail, shared workspaces and executive environments, business process workflow applications.

2. Why were game systems the leaders in multimedia? (2 marks)

The market is very large and quality demands, though intense, are not crucial to success.

3. What is a set-top box? (2 marks)

The next-generation digital system connecting the digital network to the TV and home appliances, providing interactive services.

4. Differentiate shared workspace and shared executive environment. (3 marks)

Output of one application shown remotely vs the same application run locally on each workstation with the same data.

5. Differentiate dedicated, departmental and enterprise-wide systems. (3 marks)

Self-contained; LAN-based for a department; many interconnected LANs/WANs.

6. Name the multimedia storage servers. (3 marks)

Database, image, voice mail, audio, video servers, duplication station.

7. What is a storyboard? (3 marks)

A detailed description by words and sketches of every screen, sound and navigation choice, drawn on paper or with a tool.

8. Name four architecture types. (2 marks)

Linear, hierarchical, non-linear, composite.

9. Differentiate alpha and beta testing. (3 marks)

Internal vs wider group of representative users.

10. List the items to include in a delivered application. (3 marks)

Media elements, runtime libraries, drivers, helper programs, installation and compression/decompression programs.

11. Write short notes on video on demand. (5 marks) (textbook)

Definition, architecture (server, network, set-top box), true vs near VoD, requirements.

12. Write short notes on video conferencing. (5 marks) (textbook)

Point-to-point and multipoint, MCU, shared whiteboard, requirements (delay ≤ 150 ms, lip sync ±80 ms), H.320/H.323.

13. Write short notes on digital libraries. (5 marks) (textbook)

Digital collections with metadata, indexing and retrieval, preservation, access control, networked access.

docs.title: Long answer
docs.text:
14. Explain the multimedia application development life cycle. (8 marks)

Five stages: planning and costing (hardware, software, contents, skills), designing (storyboard, architecture, user interface), developing and producing (rights and permissions), testing (alpha and beta), delivering.

15. Explain the components of a multimedia system. (8 marks)

Input, output and storage systems with their nodes and servers.

16. Discuss the user interface design of a multimedia application with the surveillance example. (6 marks)

Content selection constraints, adequate media; keyboard, buttons, scroll bars, joystick, direct manipulation; user-friendliness goals.

17. Explain copyright issues in multimedia development. (5 marks)

Nine protected work types; license before use; questions on use, period, exclusivity, region, authority, remuneration.

docs.title: Multiple choice
docs.text:
18. Which testing is done by the in-house team?
  • A. Alpha
  • B. Beta
  • C. Gamma
  • D. Pilot only

Answer: A.

19. The most common limiting factor in the planning stage is
  • A. Hardware
  • B. Title
  • C. Colour
  • D. Font

Answer: A.

20. Which architecture has a tree of menus?
  • A. Linear
  • B. Hierarchical
  • C. Non-linear
  • D. Composite only

Answer: B.

21. Near video on demand uses
  • A. A stream per user
  • B. Staggered starts on shared channels
  • C. No server
  • D. Only CD-ROM

Answer: B.

docs.title: Types and Components of Multimedia Systems
docs.text: Unit 12Notes2 min read

docs.title: Types of multimedia systems
docs.text: Type Description Home / entertainment systems Mostly interactive but not live; the interaction is completely pre-programmed. May include a PC and a set-top box plus a TV, connected to a cable service or an Internet service Business systems: dedicated Creation, storage and manipulation of multimedia objects happen completely within the system Business systems: departmental Use a LAN for shared object storage management and processing; support a specific business process shared by most users in the department Business systems: enterprise-wide Many LANs and WANs interconnected; share departmental or enterprise-level storage and processing; support local, departmental and inter-departmental applications

docs.title: Components of a multimedia system
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    I["Input systems"] --> S["Storage systems"] --> O["Output systems"]

docs.title: Multimedia input systems
docs.text: Node Role Scanning node Captures still images and document images User workstation May serve as voice and video input node Video capture node Needed because video capture needs special hardware and software Professional studio For high-quality, professional multimedia objects

docs.title: Multimedia output systems
docs.text: Node Role User workstation Output node for text, graphics, image, audio, video Teleconferencing studio A professional studio with multiple monitors, sound systems and channel-switching controls Print server Hard-copy output of text, graphics and images Fax server Data arriving through the telephone channel Gateway nodes Communication with other systems

docs.title: Multimedia storage systems
docs.text:
Need large on-line storage as well as near-line and off-line storage, and the ability to duplicate objects.

Server Role Database server Normal database needs of a multimedia application Image server Storage and indexing of document images and graphics Voice mail server Voice messages Audio server Manages digitised voice and audio objects; can do isochronous playback Video server Must maintain constant playback speed and handle very large data volumes Duplication station High-speed duplication to recordable CDs, optical disks, etc.

Exam tip

"List the components of a multimedia system" = input (scanner, workstation, video capture, studio), storage (the six servers), output (workstation, teleconferencing studio, print, fax, gateway).

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
Differentiate dedicated, departmental and enterprise-wide business systems.

Dedicated: all inside one system. Departmental: LAN-based shared storage and processing for a department. Enterprise-wide: many interconnected LANs and WANs.

Why does a video server differ from an image server?

It must keep a constant playback rate and handle very large data volumes.
